paper_title: Plausible but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of LLMs as Synthetic Survey Respondents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic survey respondents, but existing evaluations ask whether answers look plausible at the individual level. We argue the right question is psychometric: do LLMs preserve the joint distribution, latent structure, reliability, mediation pathways, and demographic effects of real human survey data? We introduce a Lithuanian organisational-psychology dataset (n=263 employees; Dunham Attitudes Toward Change, UWES-17, Koopmans IWPQ; 68 items, 12 subscales) and condition a 37-model lineup spanning OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and twelve open-weight families on real respondent profiles under a five-level persona-disclosure ladder, presentation and reasoning-effort ablations, counterfactual demographic swaps (gender, role, education), a cross-language check, and a verbatim-recall memorization probe. The resulting Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) is anchored against five non-LLM statistical baselines and a held-out human-vs-human ceiling, with respondent-bootstrap confidence intervals and an item-permutation null for Tucker's phi. LLMs reproduce the qualitative direction of human psychometric relationships, but a Gaussian-copula baseline beats every LLM on the sample-driven PSS components; the LLM "crowd" is more similar to itself (mean inter-LLM PSS 0.73) than to humans; and memorization does not drive the leaderboard (recall-PSS rank correlation 0.00). Counterfactual swaps reveal education-driven effects (mean |d|=0.56) that dwarf gender (0.12) and role (0.18); Tucker's phi on UWES falls inside the permutation null for 8 of 37 models. Downstream, every LLM shows a strong acquiescence shift (+0.84 SD), synthetic-trained regressors lose predictive validity on held-out humans (mean R^2 -0.18 vs 0.28), and models fabricate indirect effects on 3 of 10 placebo mediation paths. LLM samples are not a drop-in replacement for human survey data.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic survey respondents in social science, but existing evaluations mostly ask whether individual answers look plausible. We ask stricter, psychometric question: do LLMs preserve the joint distribution, latent structure, reliability, mediation pathways, and demographic effects of real human survey data? We introduce an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology dataset (n=263 employees; three validated instruments; 68 items, 12 subscales) [19] and condition 37 LLMs spanning OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and twelve open-weight families on real respondent profiles under five-level persona-disclosure ladder, presentation, reasoning-effort, and cross-language ablations, counterfactual demographic swaps on three axes, and verbatim-recall memorization probe. The resulting Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) is anchored against five non-LLM statistical baselines and held-out human-vs-human ceiling. LLMs reproduce the qualitative direction of human psychometric relationships, but on the sample-driven PSS components (distribution, correlation, reliability) Gaussian-copula baseline beats every LLM (overall copula PSS 0.69 vs. best-LLM 0.71, both far below the 0.825 ceiling); the LLM crowd is more internally homogeneous (mean inter-LLM PSS 0.73) than it is similar to humans; and the memorization probe rules out training-data recall as the driver (worst-case verbatim recall 4.7%, rank correlation with PSS 0.00). Counterfactual swaps reveal education-driven causal effects (mean d=0.56, max 1.50) that dwarf role (0.18) and gender (0.12) effects, the latter fabricated relative to null human contrast, and Tuckers φ falls inside an item-permutation null for 8 of 37 models on UWES despite raw values up to 0.86. Downstream, synthetic respondents show +0.84 SD acquiescence shift, lose predictive validity on held-out humans (mean R2= 0.18 vs. 0.28), and fabricate significant indirect effects on 3 of 10 null mediation paths. LLM samples are therefore not drop-in replacement for human survey data. The dataset, evaluation harness, and incrementally extensible pipeline will be released upon publication.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Survey-based research is expensive, slow, and increasingly difficult to scale: typical organisational psychology studies recruit few hundred participants over weeks or months, with informed-consent procedures, ethics review, translation work, and the practicalities of running survey panel in small national labour market. The recent availability of Preprint. A. Human reference B. Synthetic generation C. Anchored evaluation human sample (n=263) Lithuanian employees 3 validated instruments 68 items, 12 subscales 37 LLMs OpenAI, Anthropic, Google + 22 open-weight models six-dimensional PSS distribution, correlation, reliability, mediation, group effects, construct fidelity (Tuckers φ + null) 11-field profile cards demographics only, no item responses experimental factors persona ladder C0C4 3 modes, LTEN, effort 3 demographic swaps 5 statistical baselines marginal, MVN, copula, stratum-mean, k-NN + respondent-bootstrap CIs held-out human split PSS ceiling 0. 65k questionnaires synthetic, JSON-validated grid + swaps + repeats + ablations key result copula 0.69 best LLM 0.71 human ceiling 0.825 inter-LLM 0.73 > best LLMhuman Figure 1: Overview of the benchmark. (A) real Lithuanian organisational-psychology sample (n=263, 68 items, 12 subscales) provides the ground truth, the persona profile cards, and held-out human-vs-human PSS ceiling. (B) 37 LLMs are conditioned on the profile cards under persona-disclosure ladder, presentation, reasoning-effort, cross-language, and counterfactual-swap factors, producing 65k validated synthetic questionnaires. (C) Each (model, condition) cell is scored on six-dimensional Psychometric Similarity Score anchored against five statistical baselines and the human ceiling. The anchoring is what produces the key result: the best LLM barely beats Gaussian copula with no language model at all, and LLMs agree with one another more than any of them agrees with humans. capable instruction-following LLMs has prompted wave of work that uses LLMs as synthetic respondents: the model is asked to answer as person with profile and its responses are treated as pseudo-data [2, 13, 1, 17]. Concrete near-term use cases include (i) pilot studies that need fast direction-of-effect estimates before committing to real-recruitment design, (ii) instrument-prototyping work that compares candidate item wordings without burning fresh sample on each iteration, (iii) sensitivity-analysis power calculations under several plausible effect-size assumptions, (iv) sample augmentation in low-base-rate or hard-to-reach populations, (v) red-team audits of new instruments for demographic bias or stereotype leakage before the instrument enters production, and (vi) pure cost replacement of human samples [7]. Each of these uses places different load on the synthetic respondents: pilot study cares about direction of effect; power analysis cares about effect-size magnitude and variance; bias audit cares about counterfactual sensitivity; and replacement use cares about every property of the joint distribution simultaneously. The first questions of this paper are therefore (a) which of these properties do current LLMs actually preserve, and (b) which preservation level given downstream use can rely on. Whether reliable is the right adjective is contested. Recent work has shown that LLMs reflect narrow slice of human opinion [18, 9], fail to portray identity groups consistently [24], and can produce surface-similar but distributionally distinct responses [4]. Most of these analyses operate at the level of single items, marginal effects on one or two demographic contrasts, or aggregate effect sizes. From measurement-theoretic point of view this is partial audit: synthetic respondent that produces correct item means but incorrect item covariance still inflates Type error in any analysis that conditions on multi-item scale score, and respondent that produces correct subscale means but incorrect inter-subscale correlations breaks every downstream causal mediation that touches multiple constructs at once. Psychometrics, the science of measurement, asks stricter question: do the responses behave like measured construct? scale is psychometrically valid only if its items co-vary in the predicted way (correlation structure), if they jointly reflect latent factor (factor structure), if the resulting score is stable across raters (reliability), and if it relates to other constructs as theory predicts (mediation, group differences). An LLM that reproduces only item means has believable item means, not believable respondent. Reusing such an LLM as drop-in human sample then risks two cascading failure modes: methodological one, where over-coherent LLM responses make every internal-consistency statistic (α, ω, HTMT) look healthier than the underlying human data would warrant, and substantive one, where any latent-variable model fitted on the LLM-generated data converges to different solution than the same model fitted on the human reference, even when item-level marginals match. Why Lithuanian, why this dataset. Almost all existing LLM-as-respondent benchmarks use US or UK survey instruments in their original English wording, often with US-derived demographic distributions [18, 2, 9]. That choice is convenient (the LLMs were predominantly pretrained on English text), but it also conflates two distinct questions: does the LLM reproduce the joint distribution of real human sample? and does the LLM reproduce the joint distribution of the population whose text its weights have absorbed?. Lithuanian organisational psychology sample disentangles these. Lithuanian is low-resource IndoEuropean language with under three million native speakers, written with diacritics (č, š, ž, ą, ę, i, u, e, u) and rich case morphology; modern LLMs handle it competently but not natively. The three instruments (Dunham Attitudes Toward Change, Schaufeli UWES-17, Koopmans IWPQ) are international developed in English / Dutch and translated into Lithuanian for the original masters thesis we draw on so their factor structure, reliability, and mediation pathway are external constraints that the LLM has no way to game from its English-language pretraining. The resulting benchmark therefore measures the LLMs psychometric fidelity under genuinely cross-linguistic conditions, while remaining fair test of the published structure of three well-validated organisational instruments. Paper roadmap. The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 situates our work relative to the LLM-as-respondent, persona-prompting, bias-testing, and cross-culturalpsychometric literatures. Section 3 presents the human dataset and reproduces its key published statistics. Section 4 develops the six-dimensional PSS framework, the personadisclosure ladder, the presentation-mode and reasoning-effort ablations, the counterfactual demographic-swap design, the five non-LLM baselines, and the held-out human-vs-human ceiling. Section 5 reports the anchored PSS leaderboard for the 37-model lineup, constructlevel fidelity with item-permutation null distributions for Tuckers φ, counterfactual stereotype amplification on three axes, four orthogonal ablations, verbatim-recall memorization probe, the inter-LLM agreement matrix, and the cohort-stratified fairness diagnostic. Section 6 interprets the findings under five lenses (what works, what does not, what is no longer plausible, theoretical implications, and practitioner recommendations). Section 7 lays out the scope conditions and remaining open questions. Appendices AJ document the parser, reproducibility infrastructure, the Tucker-permutation derivation, the power-analysis tables, the per-model deep-dive case studies, the compute-and-cost breakdown, and worked qualitative example of LLM responses on single ATC item. Contributions. Open Lithuanian psychometric benchmark. n=263 employees, three validated instruments (ATC [8], UWES-17 [20], IWPQ [14]) plus 15-item change-engagement scale; 68 items, 12 subscales, with the documented AttitudesEngagementPerformance mediation [19]. To our knowledge the first open Lithuanian validation of all three (datasheet, Appendix N). 37-model evaluation (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google + 22 open-weight models via Nexos) on persona-disclosure ladder (C0C4, narrative variant), 3-mode presentation ablation, counterfactual swap design across {gender, role, education}, reasoning-effort ablation, Lithuanian-vs-English language ablation, and verbatim-recall memorization probe. Six-dimensional PSS framework with empirical anchors. Distribution / correlation / reliability / mediation / demographic effects / construct-level fidelity, including Tuckers φ with an item-permutation null. PSS is anchored against five non-LLM baselines (marginal, MVN, Gaussian copula, stratum-mean, k-NN) and held-out human-vshuman ceiling. Respondent-bootstrap 95% CIs and HolmBonferroni-adjusted p-values throughout (Appendices DE). 3 Cohort-stratified PSS, inter-LLM clustering, ensemble-mean baseline. Per- (model, demographic stratum) fairness diagnostic; pairwise inter-LLM agreement matrix with hierarchical clustering; wisdom-of-LLMs ensemble at zero additional cost. Downstream-consequence diagnostics. Beyond raw fidelity we quantify response-style bias (acquiescence, extremeand midpoint-responding) relative to humans, downstream predictive validity (train regressor on synthetic respondents, test on held-out humans), and mediation negative control that flags fabricated indirect effects, quantifying the practical cost of substituting synthetic respondents for human sample. We further show the gap is structural rather than prompting artifact: neither an explicit debias instruction nor in-context few-shot conditioning on real human answer vectors closes it (Appendix Table 20). Open, incrementally extensible software. Adding model never re-runs prior models; per-call disk caching and per-cell parquet checkpoints make the pipeline idempotent. Five provider auth paths (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google AI Studio, Google Vertex AI, Nexos) ship with the repository. Pre-registration disclosure. The full analysis plan evaluation dimensions, contrasts, multiple-comparison correction, PSS weights, and the baseline + ceiling anchoring was finalised before any LLM call was issued; the only post-hoc additions are the personafaithfulness check (a parsing-side change) and the bifactor summary (an additional, nonsubstitutive construct-fidelity metric). The locked configuration is included in the repository (configs/preregistration.yaml). Our central empirical claim, supported by the human-side numbers reported in this paper and the LLM-side experiments described in Section 5, is that LLMs can reproduce the theoretical direction of human psychometric relationships, but tend to generate over-coherent, low-variance, and demographically stereotyped synthetic respondents. This is more nuanced position than LLMs are good or bad at survey simulation: we show which dimensions of psychometric fidelity break down, and how much they depend on the persona conditioning regime.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: LLMs as synthetic respondents. Argyle et al. [2] introduced LLM silicon samples that mirror the conditional distribution of human attitudes given demographic profile, and reported that GPT-3 could reproduce the marginal direction of several US political-attitude contrasts. Horton [13] treated LLMs as economic agents and replicated classical behaviouraleconomics experiments; Aher et al. [1] replicated several canonical psychology experiments (Milgram, Wisdom-of-Crowds, the Ultimatum Game) with LLM agents; Park et al. [17] used persona prompting to populate an interactive social simulacrum that produced emergent social behaviours; Dillion et al. [7] explicitly proposed LLMs as substitutes for human participants in moral-psychology research. These works collectively establish feasibility: LLMs can produce responses that read as plausibly human and that move in the expected qualitative direction. But they mostly evaluate at the level of single items, marginal effects on one or two demographic contrasts, or aggregate effect sizes for single hypothesis. None of them directly addresses construct validity in the psychometric sense. Limits of LLM survey simulation. complementary line of work argues that LLM respondents are systematically biased relative to the human populations they aim to simulate. Santurkar et al. [18] showed that GPT-3.5 reflects predominantly liberal, college-educated US views, with the closest demographic match being moderate Democrat. Durmus et al. [9] extended this to multinational opinion surveys (PewResearch and World Values Survey items) and found systematic skew towards Western, English-speaking, urban populations. Bisbee et al. [4] found that synthetic samples diverge from human samples in marginal effects despite matching means, and proposed running parallel human-LLM analyses as robustness check. Wang et al. [24] argued that LLMs cannot reliably portray identity groups, particularly along intersectional dimensions, and that single-attribute persona prompts collapse into small number of generic personas. Our work complements this literature by isolating which psychometric properties break down (joint distribution vs. correlation matrix vs. reliability 4 vs. mediation vs. demographic effects vs. factor structure) and by showing how persona conditioning, presentation mode, reasoning effort, and stochastic stability each shift the trade-off. Persona prompting and synthetic-data pipelines. The persona-prompting design space is wider than answer as person with profile p. Park et al. [17] use multi-turn narrative scaffolding; the silicon-sample literature [2] uses one-shot structured-field prompts; the biasbench literature [18, 9] uses category labels rather than profile cards; recent crowdsourcingreplacement work [24] prompts for both persona and step-by-step reasoning trace. The design choices interact: profile granularity (which fields are disclosed, in which order), presentation mode (single call vs. instrument-by-instrument), and reasoning effort (chain-ofthought budget) all change the joint distribution of the resulting responses. We treat these as first-class experimental factors (a five-step persona-disclosure ladder, three presentation modes, two reasoning-effort levels) rather than fixing them implicitly. Our presentation-mode ablation in particular has, to our knowledge, no direct precedent in the LLM-as-respondent literature, although the closely related in-context survey administration question has been explored for educational test items [1]. Counterfactual fairness and stereotype amplification. second adjacent literature audits LLMs for stereotypic behaviour by perturbing single demographic attribute in the prompt. Santurkar et al. [18] examined whose opinions an LLM represents; Wang et al. [24] probed LLM-as-identity-group consistency; benchmarks such as StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs, and BBQ score sensitivity to demographic primes on artificial completions. These works typically use single-sentence stimuli and binary stereotype/anti-stereotype label. Our counterfactual design instead swaps single field of an otherwise-fixed multi-attribute persona card, asks the model to fill in full 68-item validated instrument, and then computes the per-respondent paired Cohens at the subscale level. The resulting effect size is interpretable on the same scale as the original human contrast (so an LLM on the gender axis that exceeds the resampling-noise floor where the human is null is directly evidence of fabricated stereotype rather than amplified real signal). The framework also lets us decompose stereotype amplification by which demographic axis is being swapped, which Section 5.4 shows is essential: the same model amplifies an education stereotype by an order of magnitude more than gender stereotype. Cross-cultural psychometrics and measurement invariance. The classical psychometric literature treats translated instruments as separate measurement instances that must be tested for invariance [5, 23]. Failure to establish even weak (configural) invariance means that scores from two language samples are not directly comparable; synthetic LLM respondent translated by the LLM itself faces exactly the same problem twice (English-language pretraining, Lithuanian-language survey administration). Although we do not run full Lithuanian-vs-English measurement-invariance test on humans (we have only the Lithuanian sample), we do run per-respondent cross-language ablation on the LLM side (Section 5.5) for which the mean LTEN per-item drift is 0.26 Likert points with per-item Pearson of 0.889. The published Lithuanian factor structures of the three instruments [14, 8, 20, 19] are the external constraint against which our construct-fidelity statistics (Tuckers φ, CFI, HTMT, bifactor decomposition) are scored. Psychometric measurement theory. On the measurement side, we use Cronbachs α [6] and McDonalds ω [16] for internal consistency; the indirect-effect mediation framework of Hayes [11] for the XMY pathway with non-parametric bootstrap CIs on ab; the modified RV2 coefficient [21] for covariance-matrix similarity; Tuckers φ [22, 15] augmented by our item-permutation null distribution for factor congruence; the CFI invariance criterion of Cheung and Rensvold [5] for measurement-invariance approximation; the HTMT ratio for discriminant validity; and bifactor decomposition (explained-common variance, ωh) for the relative strength of general factor vs. specific factors. Each of these statistics has long pre-LLM tradition; our contribution is to combine them into single model-agnostic evaluation harness anchored against statistical baselines and human-vs-human held-out ceiling.

sections.title: 3 Dataset: an open Lithuanian organisational psychology survey
sections.content: Original study and consent provenance. The human ground truth originates from published Lithuanian masters thesis by one of the authors [19], originally collected between March and April 2020 under the awarding universitys informed-consent protocol. The original study tested the hypothesis that employee attitudes towards ongoing organisational change indirectly affect self-rated work performance via work engagement classical XMY mediation pattern in industrialorganisational psychology and recruited = 263 Lithuanian business-organisation employees through an anonymous online questionnaire (hosted on Apklausa.lt, Lithuanian survey platform).1 consent statement preceded the survey and explicitly mentioned academic re-use of de-identified aggregated data; the original author has confirmed permission to release the de-identified record-level data under CC-BY-NC-4.0. Lithuanian organisational psychology context. Lithuania is small Baltic EU member state with labour force of 1.5 million people, dominated by services and light manufacturing; English-language US-derived organisational-psychology instruments have only been validated in Lithuanian within the past two decades, primarily through masters and doctoral theses at the countrys three large research universities. The thesis we draw on is, to our knowledge, the first to validate all three of IWPQ, UWES-17, and ATC in Lithuanian simultaneously, and the first to report the full AEP mediation in Lithuanian sample. The collection window (MarchApril 2020) coincides with the first nation-wide COVID-19 lockdown in Lithuania, so the attitudes-toward-change responses are conditioned on real and intense organisational-change context; this is part of why the human ATC composite shows substantial inter-respondent variance and why the mediation pathway is statistically robust at = 263. Demographic composition. The sample skews female (76% women / 24% men, reflecting the female-majority composition of Lithuanian white-collar employment in the surveyed sectors), age 1962 years (median in the early 30s, most respondents below 40), 33% managerial role and 67% non-managerial, with sector representation spanning IT, finance, manufacturing, agriculture, retail, and public administration, and organisation-size bands from < 50 employees to > 500. Two tenure fields (years in current organisation, years in current role) are recorded; both follow roughly exponential distributions, consistent with the relatively young Lithuanian labour market. The full demographic crosstab is included in the released datasheet (Appendix N); the post-hoc minimum-detectable-d for the demographic contrasts we test is 0.45 (median across composites), and 81% of the contrasts are underpowered to detect small effect (d < 0.3). This is the noise floor against which we read the LLM-side counterfactual stereotype amplification reported in Section 5.4. Instrument battery and translation history. The instrument battery has four components: IWPQ (Individual Work Performance Questionnaire) of Koopmans et al. [14], 18 items on 15 Likert scale, three subscales: task performance, contextual performance, counterproductive work behaviour (the last is reverse-keyed). The Lithuanian translation follows the standard double-translation protocol described in the original thesis. Internal-consistency reliability in our sample: α = .72/.80/.86/.79 for total / task / contextual / counterproductive, comparable to the published Dutch and English samples (α [.78, .89]). ATC (Dunham Attitudes Toward Change) of Dunham et al. [8], 18 items on 15 Likert scale, three a-priori subscales: cognitive, affective, behavioural. The Lithuanian translation was prepared for the original thesis; internal consistency α = .92/.81/.85/.82 for total / cognitive / affective / behavioural on the high end of published values, plausibly because the lockdown context made attitudes toward change unusually salient and internally coherent. 1The original publication uses = 261 after listwise deletion of two records with single missing demographic fields; our pipeline keeps these two records because the instrument items themselves are complete, so all reported quantities use = 263. The choice of moves point estimates by at most the third decimal. 6 UWES-17 (Utrecht Work Engagement Scale, 17-item version) of Schaufeli and Bakker [20], 17 items on 17 Likert scale, three subscales: vigour, dedication, absorption. Multiple Lithuanian translations exist; the original thesis selected the version most widely used in the Lithuanian I-O psychology literature. Internal consistency α = .93/.79/.91/.84 for total / vigour / dedication / absorption, matching the published range. ChangeEng (change-engagement auxiliary scale), 15 items on 15 Likert scale, three apriori subscales constructed by the original author from literature review on engagement with the change process (as opposed to engagement with work in general). This scale is less well validated than the three international instruments and is included in our benchmark as deliberately weaker construct against which we can read whether LLM construct-fidelity statistics correctly discriminate weak from strong constructs (see Section 5.3). 15th demographic-context block records two ordinal change-context ratings on 110 scale: the perceived overall intensity of change in the respondents organisation, and the perceived personal relevance of the changes. These ratings are used as covariates in the original mediation analysis and are kept in the released profile cards. Mediation reproduction. The published mediation analysis is Attitudes Engagement Performance with statistically significant a, b, and indirect ab paths; the direct path is positive but smaller than the indirect path, consistent with partial mediation  (Table 1)  . Our pipeline reproduces the indirect effect at ab = 0.16 (95% non-parametric bootstrap CI [0.10, 0.24], nboot = 5000, percentile method) using composite subscale scores, matching the published value to two decimals. The direction match, magnitude match, and significance match on the indirect path are the three sub-criteria the LLM-side mediation component of PSS is scored against (Section 4.3). Profile cards. Profile cards used to condition the LLM are derived from gender, age, education, role, two tenure fields, sector, organisation size, and the two change-context ratings (11 fields total). The LLM never sees the humans actual item responses, only this demographic block plus the persona-conditioning instruction text. Profile cards will be released alongside the dataset (data/psychometry/processed/human_profiles.json), so third party can re-run our benchmark on new model without re-deriving the persona schema. De-identification. The distribution CSV (responses_human_deidentified.csv) drops the single free-text industry field that occasionally contained identifying employer phrases, and rounds submission timestamps from second-precision to year-month resolution. Demographic variables are coarse-grained (gender as binary, age as integer years, education in 4 levels, role binary, sector in 6 categories, size in 4 bands); the smallest non-empty joint demographic cell contains 3 respondents. No direct identifiers (name, email, phone, IP, exact employer) were ever collected by the original survey form. Full audit trail and the SHA-256 checksum of the distribution CSV are in the Croissant metadata file (data/psychometry/croissant.json). The dataset is described in full in Appendix following the schema of Gebru et al. [10]. Table 1: Standardised path coefficients of the human mediation model, replicated by our pipeline. sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: 4.1 Persona conditioning, prompts, presentation Persona-disclosure ladder. central design question is how much of the respondent profile the LLM is shown. We define five primary persona-disclosure levels and one narrative variant: 7 C0 (no profile). The LLM is asked to answer the instrument as generic Lithuanian employee, with no demographic information. C0 is the maximum-uncertainty baseline; PSS at C0 measures the prior of an LLM under Lithuanian-organisational-employee instruction alone. C1 (gender + age). The two most commonly used demographic primes in the personaprompting literature. C2 (C1 + role + education). Adds the two strongest predictors of organisationalpsychology outcomes in the human sample. C3 (full structured profile). All 11 fields listed in Section 3: gender, age, education, role, tenure-in-organisation, tenure-in-role, sector, organisation size, and the two changecontext ordinal ratings. This is the headline condition for the leaderboard. C4 (C3 + organisation-change narrative). free-text contextual sentence (Pastaruoju metu Jusu organizacijoje vyko šie pokyčiai: . . . ) describing the type of change the respondent reported in the original survey free-response. Designed to probe whether providing the LLM with more narrative context shifts the joint distribution. C9 (narrative variant of C3). Identical content to C3, but rendered as single descriptive paragraph rather than structured profile block. Probes whether the LLMs response is sensitive to the surface form in which the profile is presented. We use C3 as the headline condition because (i) it is the most informative profile available without disclosing the respondents own free-text or item responses to the LLM, and (ii) the persona-recall robustness check (Section 5.6) confirms that LLMs do actually condition on the C3 fields, so C3 is fair test of what if researcher gives the LLM everything they have. Prompt structure. strict system message pins JSON-only output ({"item_1": 3, 5, ...}). user message provides, in order: (i) Lithuanian-language descrip- "item_2": tion of the respondent persona derived from the C3 profile, (ii) the response-scale anchors of the current instrument in Lithuanian, (iii) the numbered items in their original published order, and (iv) an explicit instruction to respond from the personas perspective on the full Likert range without social-desirability adjustment. We never disclose the hypotheses, the subscale assignment, or the construct labels of the items, following the protocol of Argyle et al. [2]. The anti-social-desirability instruction is included by default because pilot runs showed that without it, several models defaulted to mid-scale (3 on 15 Likert), which deflates both the SD and the inter-item correlations in ways that the no-profile baseline does not exhibit. Presentation modes. M1 single-call (all 68 items + 4 instrument anchor blocks in one call; primary mode). M2 per-instrument (3 calls: one each for IWPQ, ATC, UWES; the auxiliary ChangeEng scale is grouped with ATC because of construct similarity). M3 persubscale (12 calls, one per subscale). M2 and M3 break the LLMs cross-instrument context, which is the mechanism by which we test whether the LLM treats the questionnaire as coherent measurement instance or as sequence of unrelated questions. M3 in particular is the closest analogue to how real respondent would experience questionnaire administered as series of short pages. The mode ablation runs on 30-respondent subsample over 5-model subset (Section 5.5) because at the full 100-respondent grid M3 multiplies the call count by 12. Languages. Lithuanian is the primary language for the headline runs (all 68 items, all anchors, all instructions, all persona blocks in Lithuanian; the LLM is asked to respond in JSON whose keys are item identifiers, which is language-neutral). English is supported as an ablation in which the persona, anchors, and item wordings are all translated; the per-respondent cross-language ablation (Section 5.5) uses identical profiles across the two languages, so the difference can be cleanly attributed to language rather than to sampling. 4.2 Generation procedure Sampling. The headline grid samples = 100 stratified respondents per (model, condition) cell, matched to the human sample on the joint gender age-band role distribution. Stratified sampling is preferred over random sampling because at = 100 simple random sample of 263 human profiles fails to cover the lower-frequency cells (e.g., older managerial men) reliably across modelcondition combinations, whereas the stratified sample reproduces the human marginals on the three most influential covariates. The = 100 choice balances three constraints: (i) statistical: = 100 gives HolmBonferroni minimum-detectable Cohens of 0.48 for the 666-pair leaderboard, comfortably below the observed PSS gaps; (ii) economic: the headline 37-model grid is approximately $90160 in API costs depending on which providers are used; and (iii) provider rate-limits: at = 100 and minimal reasoning, full 37-model headline grid completes in roughly 6 wall-clock hours under reasonable perprovider concurrency limits. The human-side analyses (mediation, reliability, demographic effects, factor structure) always use the full = 263 sample. Repeats and temperature. We use = 1 repeat per cell and request temperature 0.7, the standard creative but not chaotic default. Several frontier models do not honour an explicit temperature: claude-opus-4-7 deprecates the parameter and the GPT-5 family is pinned to the model default by our generation client; these run at their provider default, which produces sensible responses across all 37 models. = 1 is justified post-hoc by dedicated testretest run in which we re-issued the same 30-respondent panel = 20 times per model, each draw carrying fresh per-call sampling seed so that the repeats are genuinely independent (Section 5.6, Table 15). Scale-averaged testretest ICC(1) ranges from 0.47 to 0.92 across the lineup (median 0.85), and 21 of 30 models with complete repeat sets sit at or above the human published-reference ICC of 0.78; the mean inter-repeat rank correlation across all 68 items is 0.650.97. This stability exceeds the within-LLM-vs-crossLLM PSS variance that the leaderboard reports, so single repeat per cell suffices for the headline grid. Higher would shrink the within-cell variance further, but at fixed budget the marginal value is lower than running additional models or conditions. Four models could not be re-queried for the C9 narrative variant because their gateway deployments were retired or persistently rate-limited between data-collection waves (llama-4-scout, the two grok-4-1-fast variants, and gpt-oss-120b; deepseek-v4-pro retains only single degenerate C9 respondent, which we exclude from C9 comparisons); these models retain their main-grid C0C4 leaderboard results. qwen3-7-plus, rate-limited during the first collection wave, was backfilled once its gateway capacity recovered and retains reduced effective (7294 of 100 respondents per headline condition). Reasoning effort. We set reasoning effort to minimal for the headline grid: on OpenAI this passes reasoning_effort=minimal, while on Anthropic and Google it disables extended thinking, and on the open-weight gateway the hint is passed through or silently ignored by the backend. Higher reasoning budgets multiply the cost and latency by 520 for the reasoning-capable models, so full headline-grid sweep at high reasoning is prohibitive. We ablate this choice on 6-model subset (Section 5.5); benchmarked against the testretest resampling-noise floor for the same paired-d statistic (mean d0.09 at n=100), only gpt-5.4 (and, weakly, claude-opus-4-7) shows reasoning effect clearly above noise, so fixing the default at the cheapest setting is well justified. Parser and validation. Each call goes through strict JSON parser that strips Markdown code fences, recovers the first {...} block, coerces stringly-typed values to integers, and clips out-of-range values. Calls that fail to parse or that produce out-of-range integers are re-issued with the offending response appended as an assistant turn plus stricter user reminder. The full parser and retry policy is documented in Appendix A; pilot runs show that this resolves > 95% of parsing failures, and the per-(model, condition) format-failure rate is logged in generation_log_*.parquet for the audit trail. Reproducibility infrastructure. Per-call disk caching (content-hash-keyed under .cache/llm/) and per-job parquet checkpointing make the pipeline idempotent: adding new model to configs/models.yaml re-runs only that models calls; counterfactual swaps and ablations are launched with the same machinery on top of the cached headline run. The pipeline supports five provider auth paths (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google AI Studio, Google Vertex AI, Nexos) and degrades gracefully when credentials for given provider are absent. Full reproducibility details are in Appendix B. We benchmark 37 models spanning every major proprietary and open-weight family released between 2024-Q4 and mid-2026.2 What matters for our analysis is the model and its manufacturer, not the API gateway it is served through, so open-weight models are attributed to their true vendor (xAI, Zhipu, Meta, DeepSeek, . . . ) even though they are routed through single multi-vendor gateway: OpenAI (4): GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.4-nano. Anthropic (6): Claude Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, Fable 5. Google (5): Gemini 3.5 Flash, 3.1 Pro, 3.1 Flash-Lite, 3 Flash, 2.5 Pro (with both API-key and Vertex AI service-account auth paths in the harness). Open-weight (22), routed via the Nexos gateway: xAI Grok 4.1 (fast non-reasoning + reasoning), 4.20, 4.20-reasoning, 4.3; DeepSeek 3.2 & V4-Pro; Meta Llama 4 Scout & 4 Maverick; Zhipu GLM 5.1 & 5.2; Mistral Large 3; Alibaba Qwen 3.5 397B & 3.7 Plus; Moonshot Kimi K2.6 & K2.7 Code; MiniMax M2.7 & M3; NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super; Amazon Nova 2 Lite; Google Gemma 4 31B; OpenAI GPT-OSS 120B. The full lineup is configurable via configs/models.yaml; the gateway integration uses an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API with per-vendor model UUIDs, so adding new vendor is one-line YAML change. For readability we drop the gateway tag that open-weight models carry in the released configuration, so e.g. nexos-qwen3-5-397b appears as qwen3-5-397b in every table, figure, and reference below. Reasoning effort is set to minimal in the headline runs for cost reasons; we ablate this choice in Section 5.5. 4.3 Evaluation framework Six dimensions. Each (model, condition) cell is scored on six model-agnostic dimensions. The choice of six was driven by classical measurement theory: distribution, correlation, and reliability are the three item-level building blocks of any classical-test-theory analysis; mediation and demographic effects are the two most common downstream uses of an instrument; and construct-level fidelity is the latent-variable test that distinguishes synthetic respondent who looks right from synthetic respondent whose responses behave like the construct. (1) Distribution. Per-item JensenShannon divergence between the LLM and human Likert-response distributions, KolmogorovSmirnov statistic, Wasserstein-1 distance, and the within-item SD ratio σLLM/σH. The SD ratio is reported separately because the most common LLM failure mode is range restriction (the LLM picks narrower band of the scale than humans do); JS alone is robust to this but does not flag it explicitly. (2) Correlation matrix. Upper-triangle Pearson similarity between the LLM and human 68 68 item-level correlation matrices; modified RV2 coefficient of Smilde et al. [21] (a covariance-matrix similarity statistic that is invariant to rotation of either matrix); mean over the upper triangle (gives the average per-item-pair absolute correlation difference, in Pearson-r units). (3) Reliability. Cronbachs α [6], McDonalds ω [16], and the reliability gap αLLM αH at the subscale level. We score by gap rather than by ratio because higher LLM α is not automatically better: over-coherent answering inflates α above the human value and signals exactly the failure mode (range-restricted / persona-collapsed responses) that should lower PSS. (4) Mediation. The standardised a, b, c, path coefficients of the XMY model with bootstrap 95% CIs on the indirect effect ab. The LLM mediation is scored against the human mediation in Table 1 on three sub-criteria: (i) sign match on each path, (ii) magnitude error abLLM abH, (iii) significance match (does the 95% bootstrap CI on ab exclude zero in both samples?). 2The lineup is snapshot frozen in mid-June 2026. The release cadence is roughly six-weekly, so handful of same-window successors (e.g. next-step OpenAI, DeepSeek, Zhipu and Meta release) and additional regional families post-date the freeze; because adding model never re-runs prior models (Section 4), the benchmark is designed to absorb them incrementally rather than to claim exhaustive coverage of every checkpoint. The frozen lineup already spans all major frontier vendors and within-vendor generational ladder, which is what our analysis requires. (5) Demographic group effects. Standardised Cohens on every subscale composite for the gender contrast and the role contrast (the two contrasts for which the human sample is large enough to produce stable estimates). The LLM is scored against the human reference on three sub-criteria: (i) direction match ρdir, the fraction of composites on which sign(dLLM) = sign(dH); (ii) magnitude amplification dLLM dH; (iii) false-positive rate (contrasts null in humans but Bonferroni-significant in the LLM). The false-positive rate is the most important sub-criterion because it captures the fabricated-stereotype failure mode. (6) Construct-level fidelity. Per-instrument exploratory factor analysis (3-factor solution, matched to the published structure of each instrument) with greedy factor alignment between the LLM and human factor solutions, Tuckers φ [22, 15] augmented with an item-permutation null distribution (Appendix D), bifactor decomposition (explainedcommon variance ECV, ωh), inter-subscale correlation gap (LLM-vs-human), and the HTMT discriminant-validity ratio. (A CFI invariance check of Cheung and Rensvold [5] was attempted but is omitted from the scored construct-fidelity aggregate, because the 3-factor CFA models did not converge reliably on the shorter subscales at this sample size.) Statistical baselines. Five non-LLM baselines lower-bound any LLM and let us read each PSS component against sharp reference: Marginal samples each item independently from the empirical per-item Likert distribution. This is the strongest baseline on distribution alone and the weakest on correlation useful upper bound on what preserving item means can buy. MVN fits multivariate Gaussian to the standardised item responses and samples synthetic respondents from it, then rounds to the nearest valid Likert level. MVN preserves the full covariance matrix and is therefore close to the maximum-correlation baseline; it does not preserve the discrete bounded-Likert distribution, so its distributional score is below copula. Gaussian copula fits per-item marginals plus Gaussian dependence structure and samples synthetic respondents with both correct marginals and correct rank correlations. Copula is the strongest combined-distribution-and-correlation baseline available without language model. Stratum mean returns the demographic-stratum mean (rounded) on every item for every respondent in that stratum. It is the strongest baseline on demographic effects (by construction it has the correct between-stratum mean differences) and the weakest on within-respondent variance. k-NN respondent lookup returns the actual responses of the = 5 nearest demographic neighbours of the target profile, averaged and rounded. This is the strongest nonparametric baseline on both correlation and demographic effects but is essentially retrieval system rather than generative one. An LLM that fails to outperform the Gaussian copula on the sample-driven components (distribution, correlation, reliability) is doing no better than the human covariance structure alone; this is the most important non-trivial comparison the leaderboard makes. Held-out human-vs-human ceiling. An 80/20 stratified split of the human sample provides an empirical upper bound on PSS at the given n. The training half re-derives the same six-component reference statistics, the holdout half plays the role of synthetic respondent, and the resulting PSS is the maximum perfect LLM could realistically achieve at this sample size. The ceiling is around 0.83 (Section 5.2); perfect LLM would in principle reach 1.0, but at nH = 263 the sampling variability of the reference statistics themselves caps the achievable PSS. Aggregation. The five item-level components are aggregated into PSS [0, 1] (1 = perfect similarity): PSS = wd(1JS) + wc rcorr + wr(1α) + wm (cid:0)1 ab 0.5 (cid:1) + + wg(ρdir(1d)) (1) 11 Figure 2: Human composite-score distributions for the three primary scales. Figure 3: Inter-item correlation matrix of the full 68-item human dataset (Pearson). with default weights (wd, wc, wr, wm, wg) = (0.25, 0.25, 0.20, 0.20, 0.10). The two largest weights (distribution and correlation) go to the sample-driven components that have the smallest measurement noise at = 100; mediation and reliability get 0.20 each because they are the most downstream-relevant for the applied I-O literature; demographic effects get the smallest weight because the human is itself estimated noisily at = 263 on contrasts other than role. Components are also reported separately throughout the paper, so practitioners can read which dimensions pass and which fail for any particular model. HolmBonferroni-adjusted p-values control familywise error within each contrast family (Appendix E); effect-size CIs accompany every p-value. The sensitivity of the leaderboard to the weight choice is explored in Appendix L.

sections.title: 5 Results
sections.content: 5.1 Human baseline replication Our pipeline reproduces Šarkauskaite [19]: composite means within 0.04 of published values, Cronbachs α within 0.02 on every matching subscale, the standardised mediation coefficients to two decimals  (Table 1)  , the role-effect significance (p < 0.005, [0.39, 0.65] across composites), and the gender-effect null (p > 0.4 on every composite). This is the ground truth that LLM samples are evaluated against. 5.2 Anchored PSS leaderboard Headline numbers. Table 2 reports the headline 37-model leaderboard at the C3 (full profile) condition under single-call presentation, anchored against five non-LLM baselines and the held-out human-vs-human ceiling; Figure 4 visualises the same comparison. The held-out ceiling is PSS 0.825, which sets the empirically achievable upper bound at nH = 263 and nLLM = 100. The top LLM, gpt-5.4-mini, reaches PSS 0.714, followed by tight cluster (minimax-m2-7 0.703, deepseek-v4-pro 0.701, gemini-3.1-flash-lite 0.683, qwen3-7-plus 0.671, minimax-m3 0.670); gemini-2.5-pro (0.664), the newly added claude-sonnet-5 (0.658) and kimi-k2-7-code (0.657) land just behind, while GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Grok 4.3, GLM 5.2 and the newly added claude-fable-5 (0.593) sit mid-pack. The bottom of the leaderboard is dominated by open-weight models (grok-4-20 0.362, llama-4-maverick 0.413, grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning 0.513). The 595 percentile spread of the per-model PSS is 0.480.70, 0.22 PSS-unit range that easily exceeds the leaderboards 0.046 bootstrap CI mean width; the leaderboard order is therefore statistically resolved at the headline cells. The wisdom-of-LLMs ensemble collapses to PSS 0.305 below every individual LLM and below every baseline except the marginal-only and 12 k-NN samplers because averaging across the lineup removes the persona-conditioning signal that any individual LLM contributes. The headline finding: baselines beat LLMs on the sample-driven components. On the three sample-driven components distribution, inter-item correlation, and reliability the Gaussian-copula and MVN baselines outperform every LLM: = 0.95, = 0.99 for the copula vs. = 0.52, = 0.94 for the best LLM (the MVN baseline reaches = 0.95, = 0.99 as well). The LLMs make up ground only on the distributional component (where the bounded-Likert baselines are not scored) and on the persona-conditioned mediation and demographic-effect components, which is the one place where the language-model component does something the inherited covariance structure does not. Combined into the 5-component PSS the copula sits at 0.688, close to the best LLM (0.714). The leaderboard-winning LLM thus beats, by small margin, baseline with no languagemodel component at all. This suggests that most of an LLMs psychometric fidelity is recoverable from the human covariance structure from the instrument itself, rather than from any model-specific understanding of Lithuanian organisational psychology. demographic-conditional copula. The comparison above could be called unfair to the LLM: the copula is fit on the human item responses, whereas the LLM sees only an 11-field demographic profile. The relevant test is then whether conditioning statistical generator on that same profile helps. We add demographic-conditional copula (Appendix Table 21): each item is ridge-regressed on the same 11 profile fields the LLM receives and Gaussian copula is fit on the residuals, so the generators location is conditioned on the persona while the correlation structure is preserved. Scored the same way as the other statistical baselines, conditioning does not help. It raises only the low-weight demographic-effect component (in-sample rises from 0.52 to 0.87, 0.77 out-of-sample), and the small in-sample PSS gain (0.688 to 0.719) disappears under 5-fold cross-validation, where the conditional copula scores 0.680 level with the unconditional copula (0.688) and close to the best LLM (0.714), within the 0.046 bootstrap CI width. The demographic profile the LLM conditions on adds no measurable psychometric signal to simple statistical generator. Three further analyses support this conclusion. First, an empirical variance decomposition (Appendix Table 16 reports the related discriminator; the decomposition itself is in pss_decomposition.csv) credits model only for PSS it achieves beyond the marginal and MVN baselines: because no LLM exceeds the MVN baseline (PSS 0.83 vs. the best LLM at 0.64 on that decompositions MVN-anchored scale), the LLM-unique share is 0.0 for all 37 models. Second, we train discriminator to tell synthetic respondents from real humans (Appendix Table 16): the Gaussian-copula (AUC 0.39) and MVN (AUC 0.52) baselines are indistinguishable from humans, whereas every LLM is separated almost perfectly (median AUC 0.999). The leaderboard-winning generators are the ones classifier cannot detect; the low-PSS LLMs are easily detected. Third, the gap does not close with scale: in bootstrap sample-size sweep (Appendix Table 17) the copula climbs from PSS 0.69 at n=10 to 0.82 at n=200 while the best LLM plateaus near 0.62 by n50, so the copula-minus-LLM gap widens from +0.11 to +0.19 as more synthetic respondents are drawn. Per-model insights. The component-level breakdown of the top and bottom leaderboard rows is informative beyond the aggregate PSS. gpt-5.4-mini wins the leaderboard on the strength of the highest inter-item correlation component of any LLM (c = 0.52) together with near-top reliability component (r = 0.94, second only to nemotron-3-super at 0.95). deepseek-v4-pro keeps pace through strong distribution component (d = 0.78) and the highest mediation score of the top cluster (m = 0.99), suggesting it produces well-calibrated per-item marginals and faithfully reconstructs the XMY pathway. minimax-m2-7 and the newer minimax-m3 pair high distribution components (d = 0.78 and 0.65) with balanced demographic-effect direction match (g 0.52), making them attractive for fairness-audit use cases despite lower aggregate PSS. The next strongest correlation components come from claude-opus-4-7 and claude-opus-4-8 (c 0.420.43), all still far below the copulas = 0.95. The bottom rows are characterised not by uniform weakness but by collapse on single component: grok-4-20 scores = 0.13 on reliability and llama-4-maverick = 0.36, 13 Table 2: Anchored PSS leaderboard at the C3 (full profile) condition under single_call_all presentation, sorted within each block. = distributional, = correlation, = reliability, = mediation, = demographic. Held-out human ceiling, statistical baselines, then LLMs. Top 5 LLMs, ensemble-mean, and worst LLM shown; full table in Appendix F.
