Conditioning matters: the C0C4 gradient. Persona disclosure moves PSS substantially. Across the lineup the mean per-model PSS improvement from C0 (no profile) to C3 (full profile) is 0.18 PSS units, with the largest improvements (up to 0.58) on deepseek-v4-pro, deepseek-3-2, and qwen3-7-plus, and the smallest (near zero) on llama-4-scout and nemotron-3-super, which barely respond to the added profile fields. Adding the C4 changecontext block on top of C3 changes PSS negligibly (mean 0.001, median +0.003 PSS units, within the bootstrap CI width); we therefore use C3 as the headline rather than C4 to avoid the prompt-length sensitivity that C4 introduces. We also collected narrative variant (C9), which renders the core profile as prose paragraph instead of structured fields (and omits the two free-text change-context fields), on the 32 models with usable follow-up run. Relative to structured C3, the narrative rendering shifts PSS by median absolute 0.06 (mean 0.04; the prose form is on average slightly less informative, max shift 0.22), and the C9 and C3 rankings correlate only weakly (Spearman 0.31). Because C9 changes both wording and field set we cannot cleanly separate surface form from field selection, but either way fine-grained PSS differences among similarly-scoring models are sensitive to presentation; we therefore read the C3 leaderboard as conditional on the structured presentation and avoid over-interpreting small rank gaps between adjacent models. 5.3 Construct-level fidelity with permutation null Why the permutation null matters. naive Tuckers φ on the LLM factor loadings, computed against the published factor structure with greedy column alignment between the two loading matrices, is biased upward by the alignment search: even random factor solutions can match by chance, especially on instruments with many factors and many items per factor. The empirical distribution of φ under random matching is therefore the natural null against which the observed value should be read; values inside the null distribution should not count as factor structure preserved. We construct the null by permuting the item labels of the LLM loading matrix (which breaks the item-to-item correspondence with the human reference) and recomputing φ for = 500 permutations; the one-sided p-value is (k + 1)/(K + 1) where is the number of null draws meeting or exceeding the observed value. The full per-(model, instrument) table is in Appendix D; the headline numbers are summarised below. Instrument-dependent picture (Figure 5, Table 3): 14 IWPQ: mean φ=0.821, mean null φ=0.373, 32/37 models reject H0 at p<0.05. The factor structure of work-performance items is genuinely preserved. UWES: mean φ=0.866 higher than IWPQ but the mean null is 0.771 because the 17-item / 3-factor structure produces high random congruences. Only 29/37 models reject H0; eight models with respectable raw φ (up to 0.856 for nova-2-lite) sit inside the chance distribution. The factor-congruence story for engagement instruments needs permutation correction. Dunham ATC: φ=0.549 vs. null 0.385, 29/37 reject. Mid-range signal. ChangeEng: φ=0.458 vs. null 0.301, 22/37 reject. Weakest signal; many cells indistinguishable from chance. Two caveats apply to these denominators. First, some non-rejections reflect model whose exploratory factor solution did not converge rather than converged-but-non-significant fit: on IWPQ 5 of the 37 models lack valid solution (and 1 on Dunham, 1 on ChangeEng, 0 on UWES), so the reported φ averages are taken over the converged subset. Second, and worth flagging, the leaderboard winner gpt-5.4-mini converges on all four instruments but sits inside the permutation null on two of them (ChangeEng and UWES): top item-level PSS does not guarantee recoverable latent factor structure across the board. We therefore treat construct fidelity as separate axis from the headline PSS rather than folding it into the leaderboard. Discriminant validity (HTMT). The HTMT discriminant-validity ratio (Appendix Table 11) corroborates this picture: across 37 models LLM samples violate the HTMT < 0.85 threshold on mean of 7.7/12 (64.4%) within-instrument subscale pairs, against 4/12 (33.3%) in humans the canonical over-coherence failure mode. The models with the highest HTMT violation rate are mistral-large-3 (11/12), grok-4-1-fast-reasoning (11/12), and grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning (10/12). The two with the lowest are qwen3-5-397b (4/12) and gpt-5.4-mini (5/12), which is consistent with gpt-5.4-minis leaderboard win: better discriminant validity translates into smaller correlation-component over-coherence and healthier reliability gap. bifactor decomposition (Appendix Table 19) tells the same story from the latent side: averaged over the lineup at C3, LLMs inflate the general-factor explained-common-variance share on all four instruments (ECV = +0.08 to +0.13) while collapsing the specific-factor reliability ωh on the attitudinal scales (Change-engagement ωh= 0.93, Dunham 0.22), i.e. they fold multidimensional constructs onto single evaluative axis. Mechanism. Why do LLMs over-cohere on subscales that humans correctly differentiate? Two complementary mechanisms are visible in the qualitative response logs (Appendix J): (a) persona-collapse: when the persona is detailed but the items overlap in surface wording (as the IWPQ task and contextual subscales do), the LLM treats the persona as single coherent direction (hardworking, conscientious) and applies the same Likert direction across both subscales, inflating their between-subscale correlation; (b) anchor-anchoring: when the LLM picks Likert anchor early in the call (e.g., consistently using 4 for positive statements), it tends to re-use it across items that share lexical features, even if the items belong to construct-distinct subscales. Both effects are most pronounced under single-call presentation (the default), and are partially suppressed by the per-instrument presentation mode (M2) at the cost of breaking cross-instrument context (Section 5.5). Which items are reproduced well? Regressing per-item PSS on item features across all 68 items (Appendix Table 18, R2=0.60) localises item-level fidelity in scale geometry rather than content: reverse-keyed items (coefficient +0.26, p<1011) and items on wider response range (coefficient +0.06 per scale point, p<1011) are reproduced markedly better, while raw item length carries no signal (p=0.74). The reverse-keying effect is the mirror image of the over-coherence mechanism above: reverse-keyed items force the LLM off its default agreement anchor, which restores some of the human-like variance that the model otherwise compresses away.

sections.title: 5.4 Counterfactual stereotype amplification on three axes
sections.content: Design. We swap exactly one demographic field per respondent (gender , role , education ) keeping everything else fixed, and re-run the LLM under otherwise-identical conditions. The dependent variable is the paired Cohens dz at the composite-subscale level: for subscale we form the within-respondent difference ij = swapped and report dz,j = j/sd(j), i.e. the mean swap-induced shift standardised by the SD of the within-respondent differences. Paired dz is preferred over unpaired because the only thing that varies between conditions is the single swapped field; the within-respondent comparison removes all between-respondent variance and isolates the causal effect of the swap. Under the null of no swap effect, is pure run-to-run noise and dz has floor of 0.09 at n=100 (mean over subscales; estimated from the testretest repeats), which we use as the reference for non-zero. Mean aggregates across the 12 composite subscales; max flags the most-affected single subscale. original i,j i,j

sections.title: The three axes
sections.content: (Figure 6, Table 5): Education swap (higher secondary). Mean = 0.563, max 1.499 across the lineup. This is the largest causal effect we observe: educational level alone shifts the LLMs engagement, attitude, and work-performance answers. The top three amplifiers are claude-sonnet-4-6 (mean = 0.98, max 1.50), gemma4-31b (0.84), and claude-fable-5 (0.82). The smallest-amplifier model on this axis is nemotron-3-super (mean 0.27); even this is non-zero on every subscale. The largest single-subscale effect (d = 1.50 on the IWPQ contextual-performance subscale, claude-sonnet-4-6) corresponds to 1.5-SD shift in self-reported contextual performance when the same persona is given secondary rather than higher education stereotype that the human reference sample does not support at this magnitude. Role swap (managerial non-managerial). Mean = 0.176, max 0.496. The role contrast is significant in humans, so non-zero LLM effect is expected; the magnitude is roughly 0.4 the observed human on the same composites. Top amplifiers: gpt-5.4 (0.35), gemini-3-flash (0.31), grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning (0.29). Gender swap (woman man). Mean dz = 0.119, max 0.498. The human gender contrast is null on every composite (p > 0.4, Section 5), so any LLM effect above the noise floor is fabricated stereotype rather than an amplified real signal. The aggregate effect is small and barely separable from resampling noise: mean dz = 0.119 sits just above the 0.09 floor, only 7 of 37 models exceed 0.15, and the smallest, qwen3-5-397b (0.042), falls below the floor. Where gender amplification is real it is concentrated in handful of frontier models claude-sonnet-4-6 (0.21), llama-4-maverick (0.20), gpt-5.5 (0.19), gpt-5.4 (0.19). We therefore read the gender axis as near-null for most of the lineup rather than as universally fabricated stereotype; the education role > gender asymmetry is what is robust. Universality and asymmetry. The clearest pattern is that causal stereotype amplification is universal across the lineup, but its magnitude depends almost entirely on which axis is swapped (0.56 : 0.18 : 0.12 for education : role : gender). single stereotype amplification number averaged across axes is misleading; bias-audit report on synthetic-respondent pipeline should always disaggregate by axis. The ranking of the three axes (education role > gender) is consistent across the lineup; we never observe model in which the gender swap exceeds the education swap. Why education dominates. We consider three possible mechanisms for this asymmetry, none of which the current data let us settle: 1. Pretraining-distribution skew. LLM pretraining corpora over-represent texts in which education is treated as strong predictor of work attitudes (HR literature, corporate blog posts, US-centric organisational-behaviour surveys), and under-represent texts that document the role-and-gender null effects characteristic of Lithuanian (and many European) samples. The LLM imports the stronger English-language stereotype. 16 2. Cue salience. The education field in our profile cards is single short token (aukštasis / vidurinis) that the LLM may anchor on more strongly than the multi-word role and gender fields. Smaller pilot runs with role expressed as departamentas vadovas (department manager) suggest the role effect grows when the field is described in more words, consistent with this hypothesis. 3. Construct overlap. Education is correlated with managerial role and with sector in the LLMs pretraining, so swapping education effectively swaps several correlated covariates at once. Our role swap, in contrast, is the cleanest single-axis swap because role is largely orthogonal to the other profile fields in the Lithuanian labour market. We do not adjudicate between these explanations here; the empirical asymmetry is robust, and the implication for practitioners is that any synthetic-respondent pipeline used for bias auditing must report the swap axis explicitly, because the same model produces effects an order of magnitude apart depending on which field is being probed.

sections.title: 5.5 Ablations: reasoning effort, cross-language, presentation mode, cohort PSS
sections.content: Four orthogonal ablations stress-test the headline design. Full per-model tables are in Appendix F. spanning OpenAI, Anthropic, Reasoning effort. On 6-model xAI, subset Google and DeepSeek (gpt-5.4, claude-opus-4-7, grok-4-20, grok-4-20-reasoning, gemini-3.1-pro, deepseek-v4-pro), minimal vs. high reasoning shifts the mean compositesubscale by 0.21, but this average is carried by two models: only gpt-5.4 (0.37, large effect, with composites moving in inconsistent directions) and claude-opus-4-7 (0.31) shift clearly beyond the testretest resampling-noise floor (mean d0.09 at n=100), while grok-4-20 (0.17), gemini-3.1-pro (0.16) and deepseek-v4-pro (0.16) sit within roughly twice it and grok-4-20-reasoning (0.083, baked-in reasoning model whose effort toggle is inert) is within noise. The leaderboard rank of these 6 models is largely stable between the minimal and high settings deepseek-v4-pro stays first and grok-4-20 stays last with two adjacent reorderings in between (claude-opus-4-7 overtakes grok-4-20-reasoning near the top, and gpt-5.4 edges past gemini-3.1-pro in the middle). High reasoning does not uniformly improve fidelity, so the headline minimal-reasoning default is justified. Cross-language. Same profiles, LT vs. EN questionnaire wording, 30-respondent subsample. The per-item Pearson correlation between LT and EN responses on the same respondent under the same model is 0.889 (averaged across models); the mean absolute Likert difference is = 0.26 Likert points. The drift is bounded and well within the within-LLM repeat-reliability range we measured with = 2 pilots, so the cross-language gap is not the dominant source of variance in our pipeline. The per-model best-languagematch analysis (Appendix F) reveals an interesting asymmetry: most OpenAI and Anthropic models produce slightly higher PSS in English (the language the models are most fluent in), while several open-weight models (glm-5-1, deepseek-3-2) produce slightly higher PSS in Lithuanian, plausibly because these models were trained on more multilingual corpus and treat Lithuanian as in-distribution rather than out-of-distribution. Presentation mode. Single-call vs. per-instrument vs. per-subscale on 30 respondents over 5-model subset (gpt-5.4, claude-opus-4-7, gemini-3.1-pro, deepseek-v4-pro, llama-4-maverick). Relative to the single-call reference the composite-subscale is already substantial under per-instrument mode (M2; mean = 0.270.39 across the subset) and grows further under per-subscale mode (M3; up to = 1.20 for llama-4-maverick). Fragmenting the questionnaire into 12 separate calls degrades persona consistency: the persona block is re-shown at the start of each call, but the cross-instrument context (the absence of which is the primary effect of breaking single-call mode) cannot be recovered. The HTMT discriminant-validity ratio improves under M3 because the LLM no longer cross-anchors between subscales; the reliability gap on within-subscale items widens for the same reason. We therefore use M1 (single-call) as the headline mode and treat M2/M3 as diagnostic ablations. Cohort-stratified PSS (fairness). For each model we recompute PSS within each demographic stratum (gender, age-band, education) and report the worst within-axis disparity (the maximum PSS gap between strata of the same axis). Worst within-axis disparities across the lineup are 0.072 on gender (llama-4-maverick), 0.069 on education (minimax-m2-7), and 0.040 on age (gpt-5.4-nano); the median gap across all (model, axis) cells is 0.0100.024, comparable to the bootstrap CI mean width on the aggregate PSS. Most LLMs are roughly equitable across cohorts, but worst-case fairness gaps are not zero, and the worst-case gap on single model can exceed the aggregate PSS gap between two adjacent leaderboard rows. The aggregate PSS therefore hides fairness gradient that is detectable only at the cohort level. The Appendix table reports the full per-(model, axis) cohort PSS so practitioners can identify the worst stratum for model of interest.

sections.title: 5.6 Memorization probe and inter-LLM homogeneity
sections.content: Memorization. The headline leaderboard is open to simple alternative explanation: maybe the LLMs do well because they have seen the Lithuanian translations of the IWPQ, ATC, and UWES-17 items during pretraining and are simply reproducing them. We rule this out with two-form verbatim-recall probe: direct (what is item of instrument X?; the LLM is asked to recall the item text from its identifier alone), and context-primed (previous item shown verbatim, ask for the next). Responses are scored by normalised Levenshtein edit distance to the published Lithuanian item wording. Across all 37 models the per-item high-recall rate (distance 0.30, corresponding to substantially verbatim recall) is bounded by 4.7% in the worst case (qwen3-5-397b, at 4.69%; the next-highest models, llama-4-scout, mistral-large-3, and deepseek-v4-pro, sit at 3.12%). 22 of the 37 models have high-recall rate of exactly 0%. The Spearman rank correlation between high-recall rate and PSS across the 37 models is 0.00 (no clear relationship: the highest-recall model is not the highest-PSS model, and vice versa). Three response patterns dominate the probe (Appendix J, with verbatim transcripts): Explicit refusal (NEŽINAU / aš nežinau dont know). The modal response from OpenAIs GPT-5.4 family and Anthropics Claude family. The LLM correctly identifies that it cannot recall the item and refuses to fabricate. Confabulation. Several Gemini and open-weight models produce plausible-sounding Lithuanian item text that is not the published item. Edit distance to the published item is typically 0.70.9 (clearly different) but the surface form (a single Lithuanian sentence on the relevant construct) reads as plausible instrument item. Chain-of-thought leakage in English. glm-5-1 produces extended English-language reasoning traces about the IWPQ instrument structure (The IWPQ has 18 items. Task performance: 1. worked efficiently...), revealing that the model has some knowledge of the IWPQ instrument family without being able to reproduce the specific Lithuanian wording. The leaked English text is consistent with the original Koopmans English version, not with the Lithuanian translation. Combined with the near-zero high-recall rate and the near-zero recall-vs-PSS rank correlation, this rules out verbatim memorisation as the driver of the leaderboard. PSS is therefore generated under the persona, not regurgitated from pretraining. We cannot rule out paraphrased exposure the LLM may have seen the Koopmans English version, or its translations, and reused the construct-level content but the published Lithuanian item wording itself is not what is producing the high-PSS responses. Inter-LLM homogeneity. The 37 37 inter-LLM PSS matrix (Figure 7) has mean 0.733 on the off-diagonal, range 0.4710.829. The relevant comparison is between the inter-LLM mean (0.733) and the LLM-vs-human PSS of the best LLM (0.71): LLMs agree with one another more than the best LLM agrees with humans. This is the inter-model homogeneity failure mode: synthetic-respondent pipeline that draws from multiple LLMs to average out provider-specific biases recovers smaller-than-expected gain because the providers are not as independent as the surface diversity (different vendors, different training corpora, different RLHF protocols) would suggest. 18 Vendor clustering. Hierarchical clustering on the 1 PSS distance matrix (Figure 7 in Appendix F) recovers vendor boundaries: Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI each form within-vendor cluster, with Anthropic the tightest cluster (mean within-Anthropic PSS 0.78). Two open-weight models (Metas llama-4-maverick and xAIs grok-4-20) are far outliers, sitting at distance > 0.50 from every other model in the lineup; both are also low-PSS leaderboard rows. The interpretation is that an open-weight model that is far from the proprietary cluster is far in the same direction as worse on PSS, not in complementary direction; this is consistent with the ensemble result reported below. Ensemble collapse. The wisdom-of-LLMs ensemble (PSS 0.305, Section 5.2) does not recover human diversity by averaging over models. Averaging across the lineup removes the persona-conditioning signal entirely: each individual LLM produces distinct, internallycoherent distribution under the persona, but the mean of these 37 distributions is approximately the marginal of the response scale closer to the no-profile (C0) baseline than to any individual C3 LLM run. The wisdom-of-LLMs intuition (averaging removes individual error) is therefore wrong in this setting: the LLMs are correlated in the directions in which they err, so averaging strengthens the correlated error and erodes the (different per-model) persona signal. Robustness checks. Persona-faithfulness recall (free-text role recall) rises from 0.32 at C0 to 0.85 at C2, so the LLMs do condition on the persona where it is given. Reversekeyed self-consistency is negative for all 37 models on the reverse-keyed Dunham and change-engagement items, as expected from faithful respondent. Item-order permutation shifts PSS by <0.02. Format-failure (JSON-parse and refusal) rates, logged per (model, condition) in generation_log_*.parquet, are negligible across the reachable lineup; the only substantial per-model data loss is API-availability errors (HTTP 404/429) on the retired or rate-limited gateway deployments discussed in Section 4. Numerical detail in Appendix G. Testretest reliability. To quantify how reproducible single synthetic respondent is, we re-issued the same 30-respondent panel = 20 times per model, each repeat carrying fresh per-call sampling seed so the draws are genuinely independent rather than cache-identical, and computed the scale-averaged ICC(1) treating the repeat index as an interchangeable rater  (Table 15)  . Reliability varies sharply across the lineup: ICC(1) spans 0.47 (deepseek-3-2) to 0.92 (gpt-5.4, gemini-3.5-flash, claude-sonnet-4-6), with median of 0.85 and mean inter-repeat rank correlation of 0.650.97. 21 of the 30 models with complete repeat sets meet or exceed the human published-reference ICC of 0.78, so the more capable models are at least as testretest reliable as real respondent re-surveyed. The pattern tracks model scale rather than vendor: the small/cheap tier (gpt-5.4-nano 0.56, qwen3-5-397b 0.59, gpt-5.4-mini 0.67) is the least reproducible, several points below the human reference, whereas the frontier models cluster near 0.90. High reliability is necessary but not sufficient for fidelity it certifies that model answers consistently, not that it answers like human but it confirms that the = 1 headline grid is not dominated by sampling noise. 5.7 Downstream consequences: response style, predictive validity, and fabricated mediation The fidelity diagnostics above describe how the synthetic respondents differ from humans; three further analyses quantify what those differences cost anyone tempted to substitute LLM respondents for real sample. Response style. Survey methodology distinguishes substantive answers from response style acquiescence (a tendency to agree), extreme responding (endpoint use), and midpoint responding. Relative to the human sample at C3 (Appendix Table 12), almost every LLM exhibits an acquiescence shift (mean +0.84 SD, up to +1.46 for deepseek-3-2; the one clear exception is mistral-large-3 at 0.14): the synthetic respondents systematically agree more / sit higher on the scale than humans. They simultaneously under-use the endpoints (extreme-rate 0.23 on average) and over-use the scale midpoint (+0.12). This is the response-style signature of range restriction seen from the item side: the LLM compresses toward an agreeable centre rather than committing to the strong agree/disagree responses 19 humans give, which is invisible to mean-level comparisons but corrupts any analysis that depends on the shape of the response distribution. If synthetic respondents are to replace humans, model fit on Predictive validity. synthetic data should predict human outcomes. We train ridge regressor to predict held-out composite (work performance) from the remaining composites on each models synthetic respondents, then evaluate it on held-out human test respondents (Appendix Table 13). The train-on-humans reference reaches R2 = 0.28; the synthetic-trained regressors reach mean R2 = 0.18 i.e. on average worse than predicting the mean for mean validity gap of R2 = 0.46 (worst 1.57). Only gemini-3.1-pro (R2 = 0.03) preserves nearly human-level downstream utility. The leaderboards best fidelity models are not the best predictive-validity models, and almost the entire lineup fails this test: LLM respondents are not drop-in substitute for human survey data in downstream modelling. human synth Fabricated mediation (negative control). The recovered XMY mediation could be genuine reconstruction of the human structure or confabulation that happens to point the right way. We test this with placebo battery of ten paths whose human indirect effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero (Appendix Table 14). On 3 of these 10 null paths the pooled-LLM indirect effect is significant (bootstrap CI excluding zero) while the human one is not the LLM fabricates mediation pathway that does not exist in the humans. The mediation structure LLMs reproduce is therefore partly confabulated, not purely recovered, which is direct caution against using LLM respondents for exploratory structural-equation or causal-pathway discovery.

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: 6.1 What works LLMs reproduce the direction of theoretical psychometric relationships under persona conditioning. The XMY mediation that organises the original human study is recovered, with positive a, b, and indirect ab paths, on 36 of 37 models at C3 (the one exception, grok-4-20, produces negative indirect path); the LLM-side standardised path coefficients are typically attenuated relative to the human reference. Managerial-vs-non-managerial role differences the only demographic contrast with non-trivial human effect size are correctly signed on every composite total for all 37 models. The qualitative block structure of inter-item correlations (within-subscale correlations > between-subscale within-instrument > betweeninstrument) is recovered on every model; the LLM understands that work-performance items belong together and that engagement items belong together. Persona conditioning brings group-level means within fraction of Likert step of the human reference, with the C0C3 gradient improving PSS by up to 0.58 units depending on the model (mean 0.18). The first-order picture is therefore positive: an LLM under persona conditioning is doing something beyond producing marginal-distribution Lithuanian-employee, and that something includes the qualitative direction of every major published claim about the human dataset. 6.2 What does not Five failure modes are robustly visible across the lineup: 1. Range restriction. LLM within-item SDs are systematically below the human SDs, with the median model showing σLLM/σH = 0.53 on IWPQ items and 0.44 on UWES items. The LLM does not use the full Likert range as freely as humans do, even after the explicit anti-social-desirability instruction in the system prompt. Range restriction is the proximate cause of two downstream failure modes: it inflates Cronbachs α above the human value (because the LLMs responses are more internally consistent than humans simply by virtue of being less variable) and it inflates inter-item correlations (because there is less variance to disagree on). 2. Over-coherence. The correlation component of PSS is 0.52 for the best LLM versus 0.95 for the Gaussian-copula baseline; the median LLM scores 0.37. The LLM-generated 20 68 68 item correlation matrix is structurally too coherent: subscales that should be distinguishable (the HTMT < 0.85 pairs in the human data) collapse into single direction. This is the persona-collapse mechanism we described in Section 5.3: the LLM treats the persona as coherent direction and applies the same direction across items that humans treat as belonging to distinguishable constructs. 3. Stereotype amplification. The education-swap mean = 0.56 is an order of magnitude larger than the gender-swap mean = 0.12, and the latter is non-zero despite the gender contrast being null in the human sample on every composite. Causal stereotype amplification is universal but axis-asymmetric; bias-audit pipelines that report single amplification number average across axes are reporting number whose composition depends entirely on which axes they audit. 4. Factor-structure preservation overstated by raw φ. Tuckers φ is biased estimator of factor congruence when the alignment between LLM and human loadings is itself searched greedily, especially on instruments with high-dimensional factor structures. UWES sits inside the item-permutation null for 8 of 37 models even when φ 0.85 would, under the conventional threshold, count as identical structure. Permutation correction is therefore not optional for factor congruence on LLM samples; the conventional thresholds in the human-respondent psychometric literature do not transfer. 5. Inter-model homogeneity. The 37-model mean inter-LLM PSS is 0.733, exceeding the best LLM-vs-human PSS of 0.71. The wisdom-of-LLMs ensemble PSS is 0.305, dramatically below every individual LLM, because averaging across the lineup removes the personaconditioning signal entirely. The synthetic-respondent crowd is far more internally homogeneous than it is similar to humans; combining LLMs does not buy diversity. 6.3 What is no longer plausible The recall probe rules out training-data verbatim memorisation as the driver of the PSS leaderboard. The worst-case high-recall rate on the two-form recall probe is 4.7% across all 37 models; 22/37 are exactly zero; and the Spearman rank correlation between recall rate and PSS is 0.00 recall rate and PSS are uncorrelated. The three observed response patterns under the recall probe (refuse, confabulate, leak English chain-of-thought) further demonstrate that even models with non-zero recall rates are not producing fluent Lithuanian item text in the published wording. We cannot rule out paraphrased exposure to the English versions of these instruments, but the leaderboard cannot be explained as LLMs that have memorised these specific Lithuanian items. 6.4 Theoretical implications for psychometrics The PSS framework reveals an asymmetry within psychometric theory itself that has been latent in the human-respondent literature. The three sample-driven components of PSS (distribution, correlation, reliability) can be reproduced by Gaussian-copula baseline that has no understanding of the construct at all it just preserves the empirical joint distribution. The two non-sample-driven components (mediation, demographic effects) are where the language-model contribution actually shows up. On the sample-driven components an LLM that wins the leaderboard does so by tiny margin over no-language-model baseline; on the non-sample-driven components the gap between baseline and best LLM is much larger. The implication for measurement theory is that statistics like Cronbachs α and Tuckers φ measure the instrument (its item-level dependencies given sample) more than they measure the respondent (whether the responses come from real respondent or generative simulator). This was always implicit in the classical-test-theory derivation of α but it becomes empirically obvious when one of the respondents is no-language-model statistical baseline. 6.5 Methodological implications for LLM evaluation Three methodological lessons generalise beyond synthetic-respondent benchmarking: 1. Anchor benchmarks against statistical baselines. leaderboard that only compares LLMs against one another can be entirely consistent with the LLMs jointly underperforming 21 no-language-model baseline. Adding 35 statistical baselines costs almost no compute and immediately surfaces this failure mode. 2. Add held-out human-vs-human ceilings. benchmark with ceiling tells the practitioner what the maximum achievable score is given the sample size and noise level; without ceiling, leaderboard gaps are hard to interpret. 3. Use permutation nulls for similarity metrics. Tuckers φ is one example of similarity metric whose raw value is biased upward when the alignment is searched; the same is true for any cosine-similarity-style metric (sentence-embedding similarity, code-embedding similarity, etc.) that allows reordering of dimensions. permutation null converts the raw value into proper significance test and is cheap (typically = 500 permutations suffice). 6.

sections.title: Implications for AI safety and alignment evaluation
sections.content: Two of our findings have direct implications for AI-safety and alignment evaluation pipelines. First, the counterfactual stereotype amplification result documents that current frontier LLMs, when prompted as personas, systematically produce stereotyped responses that are absent in the human ground truth; the magnitude is axis-asymmetric and largest on education. Any persona-prompted LLM evaluation that involves demographic conditioning should explicitly counterfactual-test the swap axes and report disaggregated results, because the same LLM produces effects an order of magnitude apart depending on which axis is being audited. Second, the inter-LLM homogeneity result implies that ensemble-based safety evaluations (run the prompt through five LLMs and aggregate the outputs) buy far less diversity than the surface variability of the LLMs suggests; the off-diagonal of the inter-LLM PSS matrix is consistently in the 0.60.8 range, and wisdom-of-LLMs aggregator removes the per-model persona signal that any individual LLM contributes. Both findings argue for evaluating LLM behaviour at the population level, against statistical baselines and human reference, rather than within the lineup of available LLMs. 6.7 Practitioner recommendations For practitioners considering an LLM-as-respondent pipeline for real survey-based research project, the picture from this benchmark is the following: If the use case is pilot-study direction of effect: an LLM at C3 conditioning is fine. The qualitative direction of every major effect (mediation, role contrast, item-correlation block structure) is recovered on most models in our lineup. If the use case is power calculation: use statistical baseline (copula or MVN), not an LLM. The baselines preserve the sample-driven components (distribution, correlation, reliability) better than LLMs and are cheaper to run. If the use case is bias auditing: use the LLM-vs-human gap as the diagnostic. The counterfactual swap on three axes documents fabricated stereotypes that are absent from the human reference; the magnitude of fabrication is informative about the models prior. If the use case is replacement of human sample: this benchmark does not support that use. The best LLM (PSS 0.71) is below the human-vs-human ceiling (0.83); the gap is not closing across the 20242026 model generation; and the failure modes (range restriction, over-coherence, stereotype amplification, inter-model homogeneity) compound rather than cancel. The choice of LLM matters less than the choice of evaluation framework: PSS varies by 0.35 across the 37-model lineup, but the gap between the best LLM and the Gaussian-copula baseline is only 0.03 PSS units. practitioner who picks an LLM based on the PSS leaderboard alone is optimising in the wrong space.

sections.title: 7 Limitations and future work
sections.content: Single dataset, single language. Our human reference is single Lithuanian organisational sample of = 263; external validity to other countries, sectors, and constructs 22 has not been established by this benchmark. The cross-language LTEN ablation (Section 5.5) shows bounded drift ( = 0.26 Likert points; per-item Pearson 0.889), which is encouraging, but same-respondent cross-language test on the human side would require re-administration of the instruments to the original respondents which is not available. The most informative follow-up extension would be to replicate the benchmark on (i) non-Indo-European language sample (e.g., Korean or Mandarin organisational psychology data, where similar instruments have been validated), (ii) clinical-psychology sample (where the constructs have more inter-respondent variance), and (iii) an educational-psychology sample (where the demographic strata are explicitly age-conditioned). Each would test different scope assumption of our framework. Self-report ground truth. The human reference is self-report. We cannot disentangle LLMs over-report self-rated work performance from humans also over-report self-rated work performance. The published literature on the IWPQ documents modest socialdesirability bias on the task-performance subscale; we inherit this bias in the reference but cannot quantify how much of the LLM-vs-human gap on the same subscale is due to LLM bias and how much to human bias. Possible instrument leakage. The three international instruments (IWPQ, ATC, UWES17) and their Lithuanian translations are publicly available, primarily through the original thesis [19] and the original-language publications. Our memorisation probe (Section 5.6) rules out verbatim recall as the driver of the leaderboard: worst-case high-recall rate 4.7%, 22/37 models at exactly zero, rank correlation between recall rate and PSS of 0.00. But paraphrased exposure is possible model that has seen the English Koopmans paper, or its citing literature, may apply construct-level knowledge to the Lithuanian items without ever having seen the Lithuanian wording. The benchmark therefore tests can the LLM produce synthetic respondent on Lithuanian instrument under persona conditioning rather than can the LLM produce synthetic respondent on never-before-seen instrument. bespoke novel-instrument version of the benchmark (where we would create new 12-subscale instrument from scratch with the same item-construction protocol) is natural follow-up. LLM sample size. Headline cells use = 100 stratified respondents and = 1 repeat. The choice was driven by economic constraints on the 37-model grid; the leaderboard bootstrap CI mean width is 0.046 PSS units, which is well below the observed PSS gaps in the top of the leaderboard but is comparable to the differences within the top-5 cluster. re-run at = 263 (matching the human sample) and = 3 (allowing within-respondent testretest reliability) on the top-5 LLMs would tighten those bands by 2.63 3 2.8, putting most within-top-5 leaderboard pairs comfortably below the bootstrap CI width. We have not run this because it would multiply the cost by roughly 8 on the headline grid and is unnecessary for the headline conclusions (which are about cross-model rather than within-top-5 distinctions). The full pipeline supports both larger and larger as flag-controlled overrides. Reasoning effort fixed at minimal. The headline grid uses reasoning effort minimal on all 37 models. The 6-model reasoning ablation  (Table 6)  reports paired between minimal and high reasoning, but only gpt-5.4 (d=0.37) and, weakly, claude-opus-4-7 (d=0.31) shift clearly beyond the testretest resampling-noise floor (mean d0.09 at n=100); the remaining four models lie within roughly twice that floor (grok-4-20 0.17, gemini-3.1-pro 0.16, deepseek-v4-pro 0.16), and grok-4-20-reasoning (0.08) separate baked-in reasoning model whose effort toggle is inert is within noise. Reasoning effort is thus small, mostly model-specific factor. The headline conclusions (baselines dominate sample-driven components; counterfactual stereotypes are axis-asymmetric; memorisation is ruled out; inter-LLM homogeneity is high) do not depend on the reasoning-effort default; at most the per-model rankings within the top-5 cluster might shift for the two reasoning-sensitive models. (an OpeModel-versioning nAI/Anthropic/Google model that we benchmarked may no longer return identical responses in six months). The full provider response (model name, version, finish reason, drift. Provider-rolled identifiers may drift 23 token counts, raw text) is recorded in generation_log_*.parquet for every call in our pipeline; this is the audit trail that allows future re-run to detect drift. We do not control for drift in the headline numbers. Causal claim scope. We do not claim that the counterfactual stereotype amplification we document translates directly into downstream real-world harm in any specific application. The benchmark documents an algorithmic asymmetry under controlled personaprompting protocol; whether deployed pipeline inherits the same asymmetry depends on the deployment-specific prompt structure, retrieval augmentation, post-processing, and human-in-the-loop intervention. Our finding is best read as the asymmetry is present in the bare model and any deployment that does not actively correct for it will inherit it. Generalisation beyond organisational psychology. The six PSS dimensions (distribution, correlation, reliability, mediation, demographic effects, construct fidelity) are general to any Likert-based survey instrument, but the specific failure modes we document (range restriction, over-coherence, education gender stereotype amplification) may be specific to organisational psychology constructs. Replicating on attitude scales, personality inventories (e.g., NEO-FFI), clinical depression scales (PHQ-9, GAD-7), or political-opinion batteries (ANES) would establish or refute the generality. Future work. The most natural follow-ups are: (i) replication on non-Indo-European samples; (ii) bespoke novel-instrument benchmark to rule out paraphrased exposure; (iii) extension to long-form open-text responses (the current benchmark is item-level Likert); (iv) within-LLM longitudinal stability study (administering the same persona at different time points to detect drift); (v) within-respondent counterfactual sensitivity study (swapping pairs of demographic fields and reporting the interaction term); and (vi) fine-tuning sensitivity study (does instruction tuning or RLHF on Lithuanian text shift the leaderboard?). The full evaluation harness makes any of these one-config-file extension.

sections.title: 8 Broader impacts
sections.content: LLM-generated synthetic respondents are increasingly used in market research, policy testing, academic instrument development, and in some cases as substitutes for human samples in published research. Treated as drop-in replacements they risk three first-order harms: (a) Over-confident effect sizes. The over-coherence and range-restriction failure modes (Sections 5.3 and 6) jointly produce LLM-generated data with inflated Cronbachs α and inflated inter-item correlations relative to the human reference. research project that uses LLM data as pilot to compute effect-size estimates therefore over-estimates the effect, leading to under-powered follow-up studies on real humans and over-confident published conclusions. (b) Stereotype amplification. The counterfactual swap results (Section 5.4) document large education-driven causal effects (d = 0.56 mean across the lineup) and much smaller gender-driven effects at the resampling-noise floor for most models, but clearly fabricated on handful of frontier models on contrasts that are null in the human reference. Pipelines that use synthetic respondents for fairness audits without counterfactual-testing risk certifying downstream system as bias-free based on synthetic data that has fabricated bias of its own. If LLM-generated synthetic (c) Bias entrenchment via reuse as training data. respondents are republished as human-equivalent survey data and subsequently scraped into the training corpus of the next generation of LLMs, the failure modes we document become baked into the pretraining distribution [3]. The over-coherence, range restriction, and stereotype amplification will then no longer be recoverable from the LLM-vs-human gap because the human reference itself will contain LLM-generated data. Mitigations enabled by our framework. Our evaluation framework is designed to surface each of these failure modes directly: the statistical baselines flag over-confident sample-driven components; the counterfactual swap exposes stereotype amplification; the memorisation probe rules out one form of training-data leakage; the inter-LLM PSS matrix and the wisdom-of-LLMs ensemble result flag homogeneity-by-averaging. The full harness, dataset, configurations, and per-call generation logs will be released upon publication so any new LLM can be benchmarked against the same human ground truth without re-running prior models, and any deployment-specific protocol (different persona schema, different presentation mode, different reasoning effort) can be substituted at the configuration-file level without touching the analysis code.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: This paper introduces the first open Lithuanian organisational-psychology benchmark for evaluating LLM synthetic respondents at the level of psychometric structure rather than at the level of single items or aggregate effect sizes. Across 37-model lineup spanning every major proprietary and open-weight family released between 2024-Q4 and mid-2026, we find that LLMs reproduce the qualitative direction of human psychometric relationships but generate over-coherent, low-variance, demographically stereotyped, inter-model-homogeneous respondents; that on the sample-driven PSS components (distribution, correlation, reliability) Gaussian-copula baseline with no language-model component beats every LLM; that the verbatim-recall probe rules out training-data memorisation as the driver of the leaderboard; that counterfactual swaps on three axes reveal universal but axis-asymmetric stereotype amplification, with education-driven effects (d 0.6) dwarfing gender-driven effects (d 0.1, the latter null in the human reference); that cohort-stratified PSS surfaces per-axis fairness gaps up to 0.07 that are invisible in aggregate PSS; and that Tuckers φ on the UWES instrument falls inside the item-permutation null for 8 of 37 models even when the raw value passes the conventional identical structure threshold of 0.85. For benchmark design, the implication is that LLM-as-respondent evaluations without statistical baselines, held-out human-vs-human ceilings, and permutation-null corrections systematically overstate LLM psychometric fidelity. For practice, current frontier LLMs are not drop-in replacements for human samples in psychometric studies; they are useful as cheap pilots, sensitivity-analysis lower bounds, and bias-audit instruments where the LLM-vs-human gap is the diagnostic. Code and data availability. sections.title: A Parser and validation pipeline
sections.content: We use strict JSON parser that strips Markdown code fences, recovers the first {...} block, coerces stringly-typed values (e.g., 4) to integers, and clips out-of-range values. If response is missing items or contains out-of-range integers, we re-issue the request with the offending response appended as an assistant turn and stricter user reminder; this resolves >95% of parsing failures in pilot runs. Both the raw text and the parsed integer dictionary are stored in data/synthetic/generation_log_*.parquet. Reproducibility, resumability, and incremental extension The full pipeline runs in four commands: python scripts/00_prepare_data.py python scripts/01_generate_synthetic.py python scripts/02_run_analysis.py python scripts/03_make_figures.py # needs .env with credentials Without credentials an offline mock provider can be substituted via use-mock so that the pipeline can be smoke-tested end-to-end. All file paths, model identifiers, condition definitions, presentation modes, and instrument metadata are captured in YAML configuration files. is content-hash-keyed and cached on disk unResumability. Every LLM call der .cache/llm/; every completed cells the runner flushes the in-memory rejobs whose tuple sults to data/synthetic/responses_<name>.parquet. Adding new model configs/models.yaml; scripts/01_generate_synthetic.py models <new_id> generates only the new models calls and merges them into the existing parquet. Psychometrics primer for machine-learning readers This appendix provides self-contained overview of the psychometric concepts used in the main paper. Readers with background in measurement theory can skip it. What psychometric instrument is. psychometric instrument is set of items (questions) designed to measure latent construct (e.g., work engagement). Each item is answered on fixed scale (typically 5or 7-point Likert: strongly disagree . . . strongly agree). Items are grouped into subscales that target distinguishable sub-constructs (e.g., the UWES-17 instrument has 3 subscales: vigour, dedication, absorption). respondents composite score on subscale is the mean of their item responses on that subscale; the full instrument score is sometimes sum or mean across all items but is more commonly retained as the per-subscale vector. Why psychometric structure matters more than item means. synthetic respondent that produces correct item means is not automatically useful respondent for 43 Figure 9: Memorization probe: per-model verbatim-recall rate (left) and PSS vs. recall scatter (right). Worst-case high-recall rate is 4.7%; 22/37 models are exactly zero. Spearman rank correlation between recall rate and PSS is 0.00. downstream analysis. The downstream uses of an instrument almost always involve quantities derived from the joint distribution of items: subscale composites depend on per-subscale item correlations; reliability (α, ω) depends on within-subscale item covariances; mediation depends on the cross-subscale path coefficients; demographic-contrast Cohens values depend on the within-stratum SD of composites. Each of these breaks if the LLM produces correct marginals but incorrect dependencies. This is why the PSS framework decomposes into six dimensions rather than reporting an aggregate. Reliability: α and ω. Two factor solutions can be compared by Tuckers congruence coefficient [22]: for two factor loading vectors and b, φ(a, b) = ab/(a b), the cosine of the angle between them. With multiple factors, φ is computed per factor pair 44 and averaged after greedy alignment that maximises the trace of the pairwise φ matrix. Conventional thresholds in the human-respondent literature are φ [0.85, 0.94] for fair factor match and φ 0.95 for identical factor structure [15]. We show in the main paper that on LLM samples these thresholds are biased upward: random factor solutions can produce φ > 0.85 by chance on instruments with high-dimensional factor structures (17 items, 3 factors). The remedy is to replace the threshold with permutation null distribution. Mediation analysis. The XMY mediation model decomposes the total effect of on into direct path (c) and an indirect path (ab) that runs through the mediator M. The classical BaronKenny three-equation derivation [11] yields point estimates of the standardised path coefficients; the indirect effect ab is not normally distributed and the standard practice is to bootstrap its 95% CI (percentile method, nboot = 5000). The XMY interpretation requires temporal or theoretical ordering of the three variables; in our setting the published studys theoretical ordering is AttitudesEngagementPerformance. Discriminant validity and HTMT. An instrument has good discriminant validity if its subscales measure distinguishable constructs. The HTMT ratio [12] compares the average between-subscale correlation to the average within-subscale correlation; values < 0.85 are conventionally taken as adequate discriminant validity. The two subscales of an instrument that score HTMT > 0.85 are not statistically distinguishable in the sample; on our LLM samples this happens to mean of 7.7/12 subscale pairs across the 37 models, against 4/12 in humans. Measurement invariance. Measurement invariance is the property that an instrument measures the same construct across two samples (e.g., two languages, two demographic strata). It is tested in three steps: configural (same factor structure), metric (same factor loadings), and scalar (same item intercepts). Failure of metric invariance means the scales items are weighted differently across groups; failure of scalar invariance means composite scores are not directly comparable. The CFI criterion of Cheung and Rensvold [5] treats CFI > 0.01 between nested models as evidence against the more constrained model. Bifactor decomposition. bifactor model represents item responses as the sum of general factor (loading on every item) and group-specific factors (one per subscale). Two summary statistics from bifactor fit are commonly reported: ECV (explained common variance, the fraction of common variance attributable to the general factor) and ωh (the reliability of the general-factor score alone). High ECV (> 0.7) is sometimes taken as evidence that the instrument is essentially unidimensional even when it has multiple subscales; low ECV indicates that the subscales contribute substantial unique variance.

Approximately $390 of API spend and 25 wall-clock hours for the full set of experiments, dominated by the headline 37-model grid and the testretest stability run. The per-call disk cache means that re-runs after the first execution cost nothing for alreadycompleted cells, which is what makes incremental extension of the model lineup cheap. Analysis-side compute. All analysis runs on single CPU node; the heaviest single operation is the Tucker-permutation null (K = 500 permutations 37 models 4 instruments = 74,000 factor analyses), which completes in 40 minutes. The bootstrap CI computation (nboot = 200 per model on the 3-component PSS) is the second-heaviest at 15 minutes. Figure generation is < 5 minutes for the full set. Worked qualitative example: single ATC item To show what LLMs reproduce the qualitative direction of human psychometric relationships looks like on real item, we trace the responses of three contrasting models on single ATC item across two contrasting personas. The item is ATC_05 Pasikeitimai yra idomus (Changes are interesting) reverse-keyed cognitive-attitude item on the 15 Likert scale where higher values indicate more positive attitudes toward change. The two personas are: Persona manager in finance, age 45, higher education, 10 years in current organisation, 3 years in current role, perceived change intensity 8/10, perceived personal relevance of change 7/10. (In the human sample, respondents with this profile rated this item with mean = 4.1 and SD = 0.7.) Persona non-manager in retail, age 24, secondary education, 1 year in current organisation, 1 year in current role, perceived change intensity 4/10, perceived personal relevance 3/10. (In the human sample, mean = 3.6, SD = 1.0 lower mean, higher variance.) gpt-5.4-mini (leaderboard winner). On Persona A, the modal response across 10 sampled draws is 4 (8 of 10 draws), with two 5s. Persona produces wider distribution: three 3s, four 4s, two 5s, one 2. The LLM correctly captures both the mean shift (Persona > Persona B) and the variance shift (Persona has wider distribution). The Persona response on average is closer to the high end of the human Persona distribution than the centre, consistent with the range-restriction finding. claude-sonnet-4-6 (highest counterfactual amplifier). On Persona A, the modal response is 5 (7 of 10 draws). Persona produces seven 3s and three 2s much narrower distribution than the human Persona B, and shifted down. The mean gap between Personas 46 is 2 Likert points, larger than the human gap of 0.5. This is the stereotype-amplification mechanism: the model treats education + role + sector as coherent high-educationpositive-attitude direction and applies it across items, inflating the between-stratum gap. grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning (low-PSS, range-restricted). On Persona A, the modal response is 3 (5 of 10 draws), with three 4s and two 2s. Persona Bs modal response is also 3 (7 of 10), with three 2s. The model produces nearly identical distributions for the two personas, even though the persona blocks differ substantially. This is the failure mode that drives the low PSS for this family of models: the LLM is not conditioning meaningfully on the persona block, possibly because the non-reasoning variant strips away the chain-of-thought that the reasoning-tuned variant uses to integrate the persona information. The qualitative picture matches the quantitative one: the top of the PSS leaderboard corresponds to models that correctly track both the mean shift and the within-stratum variance shift; high-amplification models track the mean shift but exaggerate it; low-PSS models fail to track either.

sections.title: K Negative results
sections.content: We report four experiments that did not produce the headline result we expected, but that are informative about the limits of the framework. Negative result 1: temperature. Decoding temperature has no effect on PSS detectable above sampling noise. We swept {0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5} on five models at n=30 respondents per cell, which doubles as natural control: two of the five hold temperature fixed at the model defaultclaude-opus-4-7, whose API deprecates the parameter, and the GPT-5 family, which our generation client pins to the defaultso their six temperature cells are six independent draws at one temperature, and their PSS spread (0.14 and 0.12) measures the n=30 run-to-run noise floor directly. The three models that do vary temperature do not exceed that floor (gemini-3.1-pro 0.16, llama-4-maverick 0.09, qwen3-5-397b 0.07), with non-monotonic, model-dependent profile. We conclude that temperature is negligible relative to model identity, persona disclosure, and presentation mode, and note that several frontier models no longer expose temperature as tunable parameter at all. We request =0.7 throughout; models that deprecate or pin the parameter run at their provider default. Negative result 2: free-text persona. We tried free-text persona (a one-paragraph LLM-generated biography of the respondent based on the C3 profile fields, fed back into the same model as the persona block) on 5-model subset. The hypothesis was that richer narrative persona would improve PSS by giving the model more conditioning material. The result was the opposite: free-text personas reduced PSS by 0.040.07 units across the subset, because the LLM tended to over-narrate the personas behavioural patterns and pre-commit to response style that then over-determined the Likert responses. We abandoned the free-text persona; the structured C3 profile is sufficient. Negative result 3: chain-of-thought reasoning trace as data. We considered extracting the LLMs chain-of-thought reasoning trace as side-channel signal of psychometric reasoning (e.g., does the model reason explicitly about Cronbachs alpha when answering items?). The reasoning traces, when present, were dominated by surface-level rationalisations of the persona (as 45-year-old finance manager would feel. . . ) with no measurable psychometric content. more elaborate prompt could surface this, but we could not get clean signal at the level of the headline grid. Negative result 4: prompt-based debiasing and few-shot conditioning. We next test whether the documented failure modes (range restriction, over-coherence, acquiescence) are merely prompting artifact that disappears once the model is told to behave, or shown what humans actually do. We tested both fixes on 6-model subset at n=100 matched respondents (Appendix Table 20): (i) an explicit debias instruction (use the full scale including the extremes; answer with the natural variability of real person; do not be over-agreeable or consistent), and (ii) few-shot conditioning with k=3 real human answer vectors (disjoint from the targets) injected in-context. Neither closes the gap. The debias instruction partially repairs surface response style it widens the response SD from 0.96 toward the human value 1.19 (to 1.11), lowers midpoint overuse (0.37 0.32) and acquiescence (1.16 0.99), and raises endpoint use (0.04 0.10) yet overall PSS is flat (0.570 0.574), because the correlation component is the binding constraint and does not move (PSSρ 0.371 0.358); widening the marginals even slightly worsens the reliability component. Few-shot exemplars are almost entirely ignored: response style and PSS are indistinguishable from zero-shot (PSS 0.570 0.581; SD unchanged at 0.96). These results suggest the gap is structural rather than prompt-conditioning artifact: the models do not absorb the human answer distribution even when it is shown explicitly in context.

sections.title: L PSS weight sensitivity analysis
sections.content: The default PSS weights (wd, wc, wr, wm, wg) = (0.25, 0.25, 0.20, 0.20, 0.10) assign 50% to the two sample-driven components (distribution + correlation) on which the LLMs underperform the copula baseline. natural sensitivity check is to vary the weights. We re-rank the leaderboard under three alternative weightings: Equal weights (0.20, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20). The Spearman rank correlation between the equal-weight ranking and the default ranking is 0.99 across the 37 LLMs; four of the top-5 models are shared. The Gaussian-copula baseline is essentially unchanged (PSS 0.688 to 0.692). Correlation + reliability only (0, 0.50, 0.50, 0, 0). This is the leaderboard restricted to the two sample-driven components on which both the LLMs and the statistical baselines are scored. The Gaussian-copula baseline reaches 0.970 (MVN 0.972) and dominates every LLM by 0.24; the top LLM under this weighting is gpt-5.4-mini at 0.731. LLM-favoured (0.10, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.30). This weighting up-weights the mediation and demographic-effect components on which LLMs do their persona-conditioned work. Even here the copula does not fall behind: it scores 0.749, exactly level with the top LLM under this weighting (deepseek-v4-pro, 0.749), and the top-5 cluster reshuffles (deepseek-v4-pro overtakes gpt-5.4-mini). The finding that the Gaussian-copula baseline beats every LLM on the sample-driven components is invariant to the weight choice. The conclusion that the best LLM is essentially tied with the copula on the 5-component PSS is likewise robust: the tie persists even under the LLM-favoured weighting, and the copula dominates outright when the leaderboard is restricted to the sample-driven components. We chose the default weights to give roughly equal voice to sample-driven and downstream components; any practitioner running this benchmark for their own use case can override the weights via configs/pss_weights.yaml.

sections.title: M Extended ethics statement
sections.content: Data subject consent and re-use. The human-side dataset was collected in MarchApril 2020 under the standard informed-consent protocol of the awarding university for thesis-level human-subjects research; the consent statement preceded the online survey and explicitly covered academic re-use of de-identified aggregated data. The original data collector is co-author of this paper and directly oversees the de-identified record-level release. No new human data was collected for this benchmark; we are evaluating LLMs against an already-existing human reference. De-identification protocol. The distribution CSV (responses_human_deidentified.csv) was produced from the raw collection-time CSV by (i) dropping the single free-text industry field that occasionally contained identifying employer phrases (e.g., specific company names or unusual industry descriptors), and (ii) rounding submission timestamps from second-precision to year-month resolution. Demographic variables are coarse-grained (gender as binary, age as integer years, education in 4 levels, role binary, sector in 6 categories, organisation size in 4 bands, two tenure fields in years); the smallest non-empty joint 48 demographic cell contains 3 respondents. No direct identifiers (name, email, phone, IP, exact employer) were ever collected by the original survey form. The full de-identification rationale is included in the Croissant metadata file (data/psychometry/croissant.json, RAI fields rai:personalSensitiveInformation and rai:safetyMeasures). Licence and re-identification clause. The dataset will be released under CC-BY-NC-4.0 with an explicit prohibition on re-identification attempts in the accompanying README; this is consistent with the EU GDPR position on de-identified research data. Re-identification, if attempted, would in any case be bounded by the joint distribution of the eight coarse-grained demographic fields, the smallest non-empty cell of which contains 3 respondents. LLM-side data. All LLM responses are synthetic and contain no information about the original human respondents beyond what is exposed by the persona-conditioning protocol (which uses only the eight de-identified demographic fields plus the two change-context ordinal ratings). No human-respondent free text was shown to any LLM at any point in this work. Compute carbon footprint. The full experiment set consumes approximately $240 of API spend and 18 wall-clock hours of provider time. We do not have access to the providers per-call energy consumption; an order-of-magnitude estimate is 50 kWh, which at the global-average electricity carbon intensity of 0.475 kg CO2/kWh is 24 kg CO2-equivalent. This is comparable to single transatlantic flight per passenger. Dual-use considerations. The framework can be used to certify synthetic-respondent pipeline as passing psychometric benchmark, which could be misused to legitimise downstream uses for which the underlying LLM is in fact unfit (the bias-entrenchment harm of Section 8). The released materials explicitly state the scope conditions under which the benchmark provides positive evidence (pilot studies, sensitivity-analysis lower bounds, bias-audit instruments) and the scope conditions under which it does not (drop-in replacement of human samples).

sections.title: N Datasheet for the Lithuanian Organisational Psychology Survey
sections.content: (2020) We follow the schema of Gebru et al. [10]. The raw dataset is shipped with this submission as data/psychometry/raw/responses_human_raw.csv; pre-processed item, demographic and composite frames live under data/psychometry/processed/. Motivation For what purpose was the dataset created? To study the relationship between attitudes towards organisational change, work engagement, and self-rated work performance among Lithuanian-speaking employees, in the context of masters thesis [19]. The original author intended the data to be reusable as Lithuanian-language validation sample for the three instruments. Who created it? The original collection was conducted as part of the cited thesis [19]; re-release for this benchmark is performed with informed consent from participants for academic re-use, obtained by the original data collector. Composition What do the instances represent? Each row is one anonymous online survey respondent: an adult employee in Lithuanian business organisations who completed 68-item Lithuanian-language self-report questionnaire spanning three validated psychometric instruments (Dunham Attitudes Toward Change, Schaufeli UWES-17 Work Engagement, Koopmans IWPQ Work Performance), plus 15-item exploratory change-engagement scale and small block of single-item demographic and contextual fields. How many? = 263 fully-completed responses (the original publication uses = 261 after listwise deletion; we 49 keep two additional fully-completed responses). Sampling. non-probabilistic convenience sample drawn through professional and personal networks during MarchApril 2020. Sensitive content. The dataset contains coarse demographic fields (gender, age range, education level, role category, tenure ranges, sector, organisation size). It does not contain names, free-text identifiable comments, IP addresses, or geolocation finer than Lithuania. Missing data. 1.4% of item-level cells are missing; the loader imputes scale-mean only at composite-score time and never at item level.

sections.title: Collection process
sections.content: How was data acquired? Online questionnaire (Apklausa.lt) hosted by the original author. Was an ethics review performed? The original masters thesis received standard institutional supervision at the awarding university (see [19]). Informed consent. Yes consent statement preceded the questionnaire. The consent included the possibility of academic re-use of de-identified, aggregated data; participants could exit the survey at any time. Compensation. None. Pre-processing / cleaning / labeling We re-derived numeric Likert scores from the original spreadsheet by mapping Lithuanian anchor strings to integers, harmonised binary fields, and computed composite scores using the documented scoring keys for each instrument. The processed parquet files in data/processed/ expose item-level integers, respondent-level demographics frame, and composite-score frame; the raw CSV is included verbatim for full reproducibility. Uses Has it been used before? Yes as the human ground truth in this benchmark, and earlier as the analytic sample of the original masters thesis [19]. Other potential uses. Lithuanian-language validation work on the three instruments; sociolinguistic / cross-cultural studies of survey response styles; benchmarking translation-based survey tools. Distribution Will the dataset be made public? Yes, under CC BY-NC 4.0 licence (academic, non-commercial), redistributed alongside this benchmark. Maintenance The dataset will be hosted in the same GitHub repository as the evaluation harness, with version-tagged releases. Errata, additional language validations, and alternative cleanings will be filed as issues on that repository. Author contact email is in the repository README.md.
